Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, depth-based checks halt blocked segments, and measured execution feedback guides subsequent decisions. This closed loop sustains search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific training. SimpleUAV achieves 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, compared with 23.80% and 3.20% for the strongest prior baselines, respectively. With limited benchmark-specific adaptation, the same core agent transfers to aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across all three splits under L1 assistance. These results establish a strong baseline for evaluating when additional architectural complexity benefits aerial search.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ABRA: Teleporting Fine-Tuned Knowledge Across Domains for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Although recent Open-Vocabulary Object Detection architectures, such as Grounding DINO, demonstrate strong zero-shot capabilities, their performance degrades significantly under domain shifts. Moreover, many domains of practical interest, such as nighttime or foggy scenes, lack large annotated datasets, preventing direct fine-tuning. In this paper, we introduce Aligned Basis Relocation for Adaptation (ABRA), a method that transfers class-specific detection knowledge from a labeled source domain to a target domain where these classes have no annotations, and no images are selected for them. ABRA decouples a detector into class-agnostic domain experts, obtained through Objectification, and class-specific residuals learned on top of them, and projects each source residual onto the singular subspaces of the target domain expert, without training. Extensive experiments across challenging domain shifts demonstrate that ABRA successfully teleports class-level specialization under multiple adverse conditions. Our code is available on GitHub.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Published in Pattern Recognition Letters 211 (2027) 269-280. Code: https://github.com/brunzibeer/ABRA

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Detectable by Design: Learning a Continuous 3D Saliency Field from 2D Detector Responses
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary:
The 3D points kept in a map decide whether a camera can be localized against it, and this choice matters more as the map becomes sparser. Existing 3D keypoint detectors usually define saliency by semantics, repeatability, reconstruction or descriptor matchability. None of these definitions asks whether a point will actually be detected in an image, and as a result most of the points they select are not detected again in images.
  In this paper, we define 3D saliency as image detectability: the response of a 2D interest-point detector at a surface point, aggregated over all views in which the point is visible. We propose DetField, a continuous field over 3D space that takes a point cloud as input and predicts detectability at any location around it. The supervision is the response of a 2D detector, back-projected from images onto the point cloud. Multi-scale curvature invariants are passed to the decoder at every query point, bypassing the voxel pooling of the encoder.
  In a localization benchmark that isolates the choice of 3D points, DetField outperforms Harris-3D and five learned 3D keypoint methods on objects and on real indoor scenes. On unseen rooms, it improves localization success by 7.4 points over Harris-3D, the strongest baseline. On objects, it also leads under a 2D detector not used in training. On sparse maps, it stays ahead of Harris-3D on both objects and real scenes.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: What Makes a Gavagai? Learning Visual Concepts from One Positive and Few Negatives
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Humans can recognize novel concepts from only a few observations by identifying defining visual attributes and eliminating alternative interpretations. However, a single observation is consistent with multiple possible concepts, and accurate visual perception alone is insufficient to determine the intended interpretation. Negative evidence can reduce this ambiguity by eliminating competing hypotheses. Inspired by Quine's gavagai problem, we introduce the Gavagai Benchmark to evaluate whether vision-language models can identify the attributes defining a novel concept from positive and negative examples. The benchmark consists of synthetic images depicting novel combinations of visual attributes and real images of newly described species. Using these datasets, we examine how models use negative examples to identify novel concepts and analyze the respective roles of visual perception and reasoning. Several models struggle even when correct attributes are provided, while others show large gaps when ground-truth attributes are replaced with model predictions. These diagnostic comparisons highlight challenges in both attribute perception and inference from limited evidence.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: When Position Favors the Wrong Part: Evaluating Left-Right Discrimination in Semantic Correspondence
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Overall part-discrimination accuracy can conceal failures when image position favors the wrong bilateral part. We examine whether dense descriptors distinguish the correct part under this conflict and whether their discrimination scores help select matching coordinates. We evaluate position agreement and conflict within the same target images and annotated part pairs, using a bounding-box-side score to define the conditions. We compare the original descriptors with their even and odd components under horizontal reflection, examine feature upsampling with the backbone and adapters fixed, and test candidate-selection rules based on odd scores. On SPair-71k, odd discrimination accuracy falls from 86.66% under agreement to 19.63% under conflict for frozen DINOv2, compared with 95.27% to 86.16% for MARCO. With MARCO's input geometry fixed, odd accuracy in box-side conflict was 34.12% on the native grid and 88.84% after learned upsampling and pooling back to that grid. Odd-score rules improve on the original hard-peak matchers overall for DINOv2 and DINOv3 and on conflict queries for MARCO. With MARCO's soft decoder fixed, reranking the cosine peaks changes mean per-pair PCK by +0.47 pp. For supervised GeoAware-SC, using the odd score to select the localization window center yields only 15 net additional correct matches, with 330 corrections and 315 introduced errors. Evaluating discrimination under position conflict reveals failures hidden by aggregate accuracy. Reporting corrections and introduced errors separately also shows whether a discriminative score produces useful matching decisions.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FoMNet: Adaptive Kernels Meet Contextual Matching for Cross-Modal Homography Estimation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Cross-modal homography estimation requires reliable correspondences despite appearance differences between sensing modalities. Multi-scale refinement progressively reduces the search range, but its accuracy remains limited by the ability of matching features to distinguish nearby candidates. The vision foundation model (VFM) provides complementary representations, yet integrating these features through fixed interpolation leaves their spatial aggregation independent of image content and the correspondence objective. We propose the Foundation Model-Enhanced Matching Network (FoMNet), which combines learned spatial adaptation of VFM features with contextual correspondence estimation. Patch Feature Upsampling (PFU) progressively predicts location-specific kernels to aggregate neighboring features on upsampled grids, preparing VFM representations for fusion with CNN features at different matching scales. Contextual Correlation Refinement (CCR) then jointly processes source descriptors and local correlations with spatial context to refine candidate scores before each homography update. To reduce upsampling overhead, we develop FoMNet-D, which replaces PFU with bicubic interpolation and uses multi-scale feature-relation distillation to recover accuracy. Experiments on five cross-modal datasets show that FoMNet achieves the lowest mean average corner error (MACE) among the evaluated methods, reducing MACE by 10.6%-72.7% relative to MCNet. FoMNet-D retains competitive accuracy while reducing inference latency by 34.0% relative to FoMNet.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Exploring the Design Factors of Pixel-space Diffusion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: In this paper, we introduce EiT by exploring the key design factors of pixel-space diffusion from three perspectives: model architecture, representation, and frequency domain. Inspired by Denoising Autoencoders (DAE) which perform denoising through a bottleneck, we construct a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer that performs explicit compression along the channel dimension. In terms of representation, we find that both pixel and latent diffusion transformers exhibit a three-stage representation dynamics across layers and timesteps: denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection. Moreover, earlier denoising and a longer basis lift-up stage are associated with better generation, which EiT naturally achieves through its channel bottleneck and increased network depth. From the frequency perspective, we establish the equivalence between pixel-space and frequency-space diffusion when keeping the network operating in pixel space. On ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, EiT consistently outperforms JiT (Just image Transformers) in generation quality. Specifically, our EiT achieves better FID than JiT: 1.61 vs. 1.85 at $256\times256$, and 1.73 vs. 1.99 at $512\times512$. Remarkably, EiT can be seamlessly applied to video pixel diffusion by simply extending the patch size to temporal dimension and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD evaluated on Kinetics-600 (resolution 256), under comparable total network parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/forever208/EiT

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: From Diagnosing Alignment to Joint Supervision in Multimodal Draft Training
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal drafts learn from multimodal (MM) and text-only (TXT) supervision, yet their effects on alignment and how to combine them remain unclear. We diagnose draft-target alignment through paired predictions with and without visual input, decomposing distributional error into text-conditioned and visual-response components. Drafts with similar text-conditioned alignment can still differ markedly in visual-response risk and acceptance. Controlled continuation training shows that high-risk groups outperform random and low-risk groups, and visual-response risk guides MM training more effectively than aggregate risk. Building on these diagnostics, we propose MNRS-Joint, which configures joint supervision from a given draft's component-risk distributions, using modality-specific mean risks to determine the MM:TXT mixture. Across three warm-ups, its distinct mixtures fall in high-performing regions of the ratio sweeps. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, MNRS-Joint improves mean accepted length from 3.35 to 3.53 and mean speedup from $2.04\times$ to $2.16\times$ over composition-matched random training under greedy tree decoding. The gains also hold under stochastic chain decoding.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TaCo: Rethinking Correlation for Visual Tracking on Edge Devices
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Lightweight trackers have replaced cross-correlation with attention, and on low-power edge hardware they pay for it, since memory-bound softmax, normalization and reshaping operators of attention cost far more time than their arithmetic suggests. Benchmarking efficient trackers on an edge Neural Processing Unit (NPU) and an Arm CPU under one numerically validated protocol, we find that correlation trackers are the fast ones, but they lag in accuracy unless they adopt a ViT backbone, which brings attention back. We revisit what correlation lacks. Template--search interaction serves two roles: conditioning the search features on the target and matching them against it spatially. Attention does both, whereas correlation only matches, and does so on features extracted without knowledge of the target. We present TaCo (Target-aligned Correlation), which supplies the missing conditioning without attention by letting the template enter the per-frame network only as operands computed once per video. A descriptor of the target scales and shifts the search features channel by channel inside the backbone, and kernels aligned with the target box, each with a weight predicted from the template, correlate with them in one matrix product. With the backbone fixed, our correlation remains essential while incurring negligible NPU overhead, offering a better speed-accuracy trade-off than the attention-based interactions we tested. TaCo-T achieves 62.3% LaSOT AUC at 184 FPS on the Rockchip RV1126B NPU and 96 FPS on a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU, 3.0x and 3.5x the NPU speed of HiT-Tiny and AsymTrack-T at higher accuracy. TaCo-B reaches 65.6% at 50 FPS on the NPU, more than twice the speed of HiT-Base, AsymTrack-B and LightFC-vit, again at higher accuracy. Code and models are available at https://github.com/TsingWei/TaCo-Tracker.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MulCLIP: A Multi-level Alignment Framework for Enhancing Fine-grained Long-context CLIP
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models such as CLIP excel at image-text alignment but struggle with long, detailed descriptions due to training on short captions. Recent methods address this limitation using region proposals to align visual regions with sentences, but at substantial deployment cost. We present MulCLIP, an end-to-end multi-level alignment framework that directly exploits natural long-text structure without region proposals. Instead of simply stacking objectives, MulCLIP aligns different textual granularities through compatible training signals: global contrastive alignment for long captions and short summaries, Word-Patch Reconstruction over locally calibrated features for within-sample word-patch semantics, and Subcaption-Aggregated Patch alignment for context-rich subcaption grounding. Experiments on benchmarks spanning varying caption lengths show consistent gains, and ablations confirm that the proposed objectives are complementary and jointly improve the overall framework. Code will be released at https://github.com/truongchau2602/MulCLIP.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WorldBridge: Bridging Scattered Views for Coherent 3D World Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Projector Subspace Optimization for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet adapting them to sequential tasks requires Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). Existing replay-free methods expand prompts or routed LoRA experts across multi-layer decoders, incurring heavy parameter and routing overhead while shifting internal feature distributions. Instead, we identify the final linear layer of the vision-language projector as a high-capacity, coordinate-stationary bridge, where sequential updates easily induce interface drift by displacing historical visual tokens. While low-rank subspace adaptation offers a compact remedy, selecting directions solely from historical statistics or task gradients sacrifices plasticity or stability, and unconstrained multi-step updates still accumulate large drift. To resolve both issues, we propose Projector Refinement through Optimized Update Directions (PROUD), a continual subspace optimization framework for the terminal projector layer. At task onset, PROUD combines retained input statistics with initial gradients to analytically extract a metric-orthonormal subspace maximizing first-order task gain under a drift budget. During training, it regularizes updates within this fixed subspace via an exact Frobenius penalty before losslessly merging them with zero inference or routing overhead. Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones show that PROUD outperforms recent replay-free baselines in continual accuracy while curbing forgetting with a fraction of trainable parameters.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: STEREOFLOW: Progressive Stereo Matching with StereoDiT and Transition Flow Matching
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Stereo matching is a fundamental task in 3D reconstruction. Despite remarkable advances, the prevailing paradigms formulate stereo matching as a deterministic regression problem, collapsing the multimodal distribution modeling into a single-point estimation. This formulation suffers from a regression-to-mean bias, frequently struggling with ambiguous regions. In contrast, we introduce a prior-guided generative framework that integrates deterministic matching regression and generative distribution modeling within a complementary formulation. Built upon this formulation, we introduce StereoFlow through three key components: (i) a two-stage progressive cascade matching network that progressively produces multi-resolution stereo conditions with complementary matching cues; (ii) a pixel diffusion transformer (termed StereoDiT) with a frequency-decoupled architecture for modeling correspondence ambiguity; (iii) a few-step flow matching objective (termed Transition Flow Matching) for efficient optimization. In summary, \textsc{\textbf{StereoFlow}} achieves strong geometric consistency and rich fine-grained details in ill-posed, discontinuous regions and under zero-shot generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed StereoFlow establishes multiple state-of-the-art results across benchmarks, including Scene Flow, KITTI, ETH3D, and Middlebury.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AffectWorld: Benchmarking Emotion-Driven Future World Prediction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The world encompasses both physical environments and human actors. Predicting its evolution requires understanding both physical laws and how emotions shape human actions. However, existing world model benchmarks primarily assess physical plausibility and perceptual quality, leaving emotion-driven world evolution largely untested. We introduce AffectWorld, a benchmark that evaluates the chain Emotion - Action - World State through three tasks: World-State Consistency, Emotion-Action Consistency, and Causal Consistency. It comprises 1,498 everyday video samples annotated with plausible emotions, action tendencies, and atomic world-state constraints. A counterfactual subset of 223 samples tests whether changing an agent's emotion under fixed scene and event conditions yields corresponding changes in actions and consequences. We define seven metrics across the three tasks and an additional counterfactual metric, combining automatic visual assessment with human-calibrated VLM/LLM judgments. Evaluations of eight SoTA world models (e.g., Cosmos 3) required world-state change scores of 0.064-0.240 and counterfactual emotion sensitivity scores of 0.027-0.070 on a [0, 1] scale. These results reveal substantial gaps in generating the consequences of emotion-driven actions and adapting future predictions to emotional interventions. AffectWorld provides a testbed for advancing world models that capture how emotions shape future physical and social states\footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AffectWorld-Benchmark-370C/}.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Hijacking 3D Generation: Targeted Adversarial Attacks against Image-to-3D Models via Prefix Trajectory Alignment
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Online services that deploy Image-to-3D models enable users to generate high-quality 3D assets from a single image. However, the generated 3D geometry can violate content policies and cause broader security risks. To prevent such content, these services typically use policy-restricted inspectors to examine uploaded images before generation. Since the inspector examines only the visible content of the input, a visually benign image can still induce the generation of policy-restricted 3D geometry. However, turning this vulnerability into an effective attack is non-trivial in the black-box setting: global backpropagation through the long DiT generation trajectory is difficult to fit, while different image preprocessing pipelines across services can substantially reduce transferability. In this paper, we present PTA3D, a targeted adversarial attack against Image-to-3D models that addresses these challenges through Prefix Trajectory Alignment (PTA) and Preprocessing Aware Optimization (PAO). PTA progressively aligns the prefix DiT outputs of the adversarial trajectory with those of the target trajectory, where the core geometric structure is formed, allowing the final geometry to be controlled without optimizing through the complete generation trajectory. PAO exposes adversarial optimization to diverse image transformations rather than a single preprocessing pipeline, reducing sensitivity to the mismatch between surrogate and target services. We establish a prefix-to-output bound and a preprocessing-aware transfer bound to theoretically characterize the effectiveness of the two designs. Experiments on three open-source Image-to-3D models and three online services show that PTA3D achieves 41.5%-88.5% ASR on online services and 90.8%-94.6% ASR in white box settings, substantially outperforming existing attacks.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Class Agnostic Instance-level Descriptor for Instance Search
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Despite the great success of the deep features in content-based image retrieval, the visual instance search remains challenging due to the lack of effective instance-level feature representation. Supervised or weakly supervised object detection methods are not the appropriate solutions due to their poor performance on the unknown object categories. In this paper, based on the feature set output from self-supervised ViT, the instance-level region discovery is modeled as detecting the compact feature subsets in a hierarchical fashion. The hierarchical decomposition results in a hierarchy of instance regions. On the one hand, this kind of hierarchical decomposition well addresses the problem of object embedding and occlusions, which are widely observed in real scenarios. On the other hand, the non-leaf nodes and leaf nodes on the hierarchy correspond to the instance regions in different granularities within an image. Therefore, features in uniform length are produced for these instance regions, which may cover across a dominant image region, an integral of multiple instances, or various individual instances. Such a collection of features allows us to unify the image retrieval, multi-instance search, and instance search into one framework. The empirical studies on three benchmarks show that such an instance-level descriptor remains effective on both the known and unknown object categories. Moreover, the superior performance is achieved on single-instance and multi-instance search, as well as image retrieval tasks.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Added further evaluation on ILIAS Core with different detector and descriptor backbones

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: When to Respond, Where to Ground: Streaming 3D Affordance Grounding
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Given a continuous RGB-D stream and a language request, streaming 3D affordance grounding requires an agent to decide when to respond and where to locate the requested functional part using only observations available so far. Existing 3D affordance grounding methods typically assume complete scene observations, while streaming vision-language models lack fine-grained 3D functional grounding. Our goal is to jointly determine response timing and functional-part localization during continuous scene observation. We propose StreamAff, an evidence-guided response strategy that makes both decisions from the grounding model's own visual evidence. The model scores the visual patches of the frames it reads: their combined support, weighed against a wait option, decides when to respond, and the highest-scoring patch selects the frame to ground in. A conditional look-back policy lets the model answer from an earlier observation at the moment of the request or wait for new evidence, and zoom-and-refine grounding segments the part named in the answer on the 3D points of the selected frame. We further introduce StreamFun3D, a benchmark derived from real-world 3D scenes that evaluates response timing and grounding across four evidence settings: Current, History, Future, and Unobserved, together with StreamIoU, a metric that credits a mask only when the response is timely and grounded in a valid source frame. We adapt offline 3D affordance grounding methods and build external-decider baselines that pair vision-language models with our mask decoder. StreamAff achieves 30.14% StreamIoU on 15-second streams, a 40.6% relative improvement over the strongest of these baselines.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SPARC: Geometry-Guided Attention Pruning for Long-Horizon Camera-Controlled Video Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/SPARC.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LongScape: Advancing Long-Horizon Embodied World Models with Context-Aware MoE
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video-based world models hold significant potential for generating high-quality embodied manipulation data. However, current video generation methods struggle to achieve stable long-horizon generation: classical diffusion-based approaches often suffer from temporal inconsistency and visual drift over multiple rollouts, while autoregressive methods tend to compromise on visual detail. To solve this, we introduce LongScape, a hybrid framework that adaptively combines intra-chunk diffusion denoising with inter-chunk autoregressive causal generation. Our core innovation is an action-guided, variable-length chunking mechanism that partitions video based on the semantic context of robotic actions. This aligns chunk boundaries with robotic interaction events and motion dynamics, enabling the model to flexibly generate diverse dynamics. We further introduce a Context-aware Mixture-of-Experts (CMoE) framework that adaptively activates specialized experts for each chunk during generation to produce high-quality videos with coherent chunk transitions. Extensive experiments on two embodied benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art generation performance. Notably, LongScape maintains high generation quality and temporal consistency over 1,000-frame rollouts. When used as synthetic training data, LongScape videos lift the success rate of a downstream VLA policy by 9.8 percentage points over real-only training, outperforming augmentation with other long-video generators. Our code is available at: https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/Longscape.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 17 pages, including appendix. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Surf-Style: Surface-Based Scene Stylization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Consistent and controllable 3D stylization is critical for visual computing applications such as immersive visualization, augmented and virtual reality content creation, and artistic scene rendering. While 2D image stylization has advanced significantly, extending these methods to 3D remains challenging due to the need for cross-view consistency, where stylized renderings must align across all viewpoints. Applying 2D stylization independently to each rendered view often results in inconsistencies across perspectives. Existing methods attempt to improve consistency by leveraging implicit radiance field representations, which model scene appearance as a function of spatial locations. However, these methods struggle with ambiguity in updating colors, as the indirect dependence between pixel appearance and learnable scene parameters makes it difficult to enforce consistent stylization during optimization. This work presents Surface-based Scene Stylization (Surf-Style), which reconstructs object surfaces in a 3D scene and uses these surfaces to achieve geometric consistency and localized stylization. Surf-Style defines a learnable appearance model over 3D space, which is modified to replicate the visual style of a reference image. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior consistency and offers greater flexibility in controllable stylization, including the ability to target specific surface regions and combine different styles.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MidasTUI: Instant Tangible User Interfaces for Wearable Displays using Everyday Objects
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: While wearable displays can bring digital workspaces anywhere, interaction remains limited by mid-air gestures that lack tactile feedback and induce fatigue, or controllers that are cumbersome to carry. We present MidasTUI, a system that instantly transforms arbitrary everyday objects into opportunistic tangible user interfaces through brief interaction demonstrations. For example, a user can slide an earbud case across a table as a mouse, enabling opportunistic interaction without carrying a dedicated input device. MidasTUI detects when a user is holding and moving an object using the wearable display camera and a Transformer-based temporal classifier. It then infers the intended input modality (e.g., slider, mouse, keypad) from hand movement and maps the tracked hand-object interaction to an application function. Our evaluations demonstrate reliable cross-object and cross-user generalization. A comparative user study further shows that grounding interaction in everyday objects reduces physical burden and improves perceived usability and control relative to mid-air interaction.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Supporting Without Taking Over: AI Support in Gratitude Writing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Gratitude writing can support well-being, but independent practice may lack guidance. Generative AI could help while shaping reflection, agency, and ownership. We investigated how gratitude-writing format and AI-assistance mode influence well-being and writing experiences. In a 2x2 between-subjects study (N=401), participants completed a gratitude reflection or a gratitude letter using two AI-assistance modes: scaffolding, which provided reflective questions after inactivity, or co-writing, which offered inline text suggestions. Participants' well-being improved after using our AI-assisted gratitude-writing system, consistent with the activity's intended benefits. However, participants' experiences revealed a trade-off between the AI-support types: co-writing received higher usability ratings, yet its immediacy could disrupt writing, and greater suggestion acceptance was associated with weaker perceived agency. Scaffolding supported stronger perceived human ownership but was sometimes overlooked. These findings extend human-AI writing research beyond productivity and text quality by showing how AI involvement shapes psychological outcomes and the experience of self-guided, emotionally meaningful writing.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Tap-to-Adapt: Learning User-Aligned Response Timing for Speech Agents
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Aligning speech agents' response initiation with users' expectations remains challenging. We introduce Tap-to-Adapt, a framework for interactive speech systems in which manual activation and interruption provide both immediate response control and online supervision for personalized initiation timing. To learn from sparse corrections and recent feedback, we introduce \emph{Balanced Proximal Replay for History-conditioned Timing} (BPRHT) as its response initiation timing control mechanism, combining frozen speech representations, class-balanced replay with proximal regularization, and recent correction history. We evaluate acoustic backbones for BPRHT on recorded speech and compare update rules and recent-history configurations in simulation. The selected replay and history mechanisms lower simulated correction rates relative to their respective baselines. To reduce new users' cold-start correction burden, we evaluate shared initialization in a two-stage user study. Stage~1 established shared initialization with 20 participants, locking the average of earlier participants' final heads upon parameter and opening-correction plateaus. Stage~2 assigned 48 new participants equally to online adaptation with or without shared initialization, or frozen shared initialization. Online adaptation without shared initialization had more opening corrections per minute than with it (rate ratio 1.69, 95\% confidence interval 1.15--2.49). Final-block correction rates were similar across conditions. Online updates accompanied reported speaking and waiting adjustments. Declining corrections under frozen parameters also suggest user accommodation. Code and 1,000 labeled pilot recordings are available at: https://github.com/ZihongHe/tap_to_adapt

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Procedure Inference as Memory: Learning Recruiter Decision Procedures from OKF-Structured Episodes in Multi-Session Hiring Assistants
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4.
  In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection.
  On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Includes supplementary appendices with experimental configurations, prompts, evaluation protocols, and learned procedure examples

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Decision-Aligned Value Learning for Selective Adoption of EEG Fusion in Human-Robot Collaboration
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural activity associated with human perception and decision-making. It provides human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems with measurable evidence for event recognition, situation assessment, and action preparation. External sensing cannot easily provide such evidence. However, the quality and complementarity of this evidence vary across samples, and existing EEG fusion methods do not explicitly determine when EEG improves a prediction. We therefore framed selective EEG use as a sample-wise incremental-value estimation problem and proposed Value Estimation and Constraint-Aware Triage for Adoption (VECTA). VECTA separates the generation of an EEG-informed Fusion prediction from the decision about whether it should replace the existing Base prediction. The framework uses system gain to quantify the loss reduction from Base to Fusion and matching gain to assess whether benefits arise from sample-matched EEG. A signed-value learner estimates system gain from decision-time evidence and prioritizes high-value Fusion outputs under budget constraints. Cross-subject evaluations on three HRC datasets showed that matched Fusion outperformed shuffled controls. Estimated gains tracked realized gains, with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612 and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.708-0.842. Under budget constraints, VECTA reduced Brier loss and harmful Fusion adoption and achieved the highest mean normalized AUBC across three datasets among the selective-decision methods evaluated. Validation on three external multi-modal datasets showed that VECTA could be applied directly as a post-hoc decision layer to task-specific predictors without retraining. These results show that selective Fusion adoption can translate the uneven utility of EEG into system-level gains.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: RecField: Embedding Recommendations into Spatial Movie Organization as Affordances for Serendipitous Encounters
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Research on serendipity-oriented recommender systems has focused on algorithms that recommend unexpected yet useful items. However, serendipity is increasingly viewed as a user experience shaped by both algorithmic outputs and system features. This study positions recommendations not as the primary goal users pursue but as an environmental affordance that creates opportunities for discovery during other activities. We propose RecField, a spatial movie organization interface where users freely arrange movies into collection zones. For each collection, RecField provides attribute-based recommendation lists labeled according to their recommendation perspectives. A between-subjects experiment ($N$ = 57) examined the effects of recommendations on discoveries made during a foreground task of creating and organizing personal movie profiles. Although recommendations did not significantly affect environment-level perceived serendipity, ratings of encounter-related aspects tended to be higher, with small effect sizes. At the individual-movie level, favorites in the recommendation condition received significantly higher ratings for stimulating the desire to watch and broadening preferences, but not for novelty or unexpectedness. Notably, only 14\% of evaluated favorites in the recommendation condition were added directly from recommendation lists. Differences in ratings showed similar effect sizes even when the analysis was restricted to favorites added through other routes. These findings suggest that embedded recommendations can contribute to serendipitous experiences both directly through item acceptance and indirectly by prompting users' own exploration and re-evaluation. They also highlight the value of evaluating serendipity at both the environment and item levels and the limitations of relying solely on direct recommendation acceptance rates.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted speculation about a new job role: the prompt engineer. However, empirical evidence on how common such positions are and what skills employers expect of them remains scarce. In this paper, we present a data-driven analysis of a snapshot of LinkedIn job postings for data and AI roles taken in April 2025, after LLMs had entered everyday work but before LLM-based agents became widely adopted. We analyzed 20,662 job postings on LinkedIn for prompt engineers (72 postings) and four established data and AI roles: data scientist, data engineer, data analyst, and machine learning engineer. We find that prompt engineer roles were rare even at this point in time, making up less than 0.5% of the postings across the five roles we sampled. Because our snapshot predates the widespread adoption of LLM-based agents, we argue that the data captures the role of prompt engineer under favorable conditions. Whether its share has since declined is an open question that later snapshots can test. Despite its rarity, prompt engineering has a distinct skill profile. Prompt engineer postings emphasize AI knowledge (22.8%), communication (21.9%), prompt design (18.7%), and creative problem-solving (15.8%). These soft and hard skill requirements differ significantly from those of the four established roles. Taken together, the distinct skill profile and the scarcity of dedicated postings suggest that prompt engineering is best understood not as a profession of its own, but as a distinct skill that is useful across many professions. Our findings inform job seekers, employers, and educators about how to position prompt engineering in the evolving AI workforce.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: On Semiotic-Grounded Interpretive Evaluation of Generative Art
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Interpretation is essential to deciphering the language of art: audiences communicate with artists by recovering meaning from visual artifacts. However, current Generative Art (GenArt) evaluators primarily emphasize surface-level image quality or literal prompt adherence, failing to assess the deeper symbolic or contextual meaning intended by the creator. We formalize this observation using Peircean computational semiotic theory that models Human-GenArt Interaction (HGI) as cascaded semiosis. This framework reveals that artistic meaning is conveyed through iconic, symbolic, and indexical modes, whereas appearance-centered evaluators tend to emphasize the iconic mode. Building on this account, we propose SemJudge, an interpretation-centric evaluation framework that uses a Hierarchical Semiosis Graph (HSG) to reconstruct meaning conveyance from prompt to generated artifact. Experiments on an interpretation-intensive benchmark, SemiosisArt, show that SemJudge aligns more closely with human judgments than existing baselines. User studies further demonstrate that SemJudge produces deeper, more insightful artistic interpretations. We hope these findings pave the way for GenArt to move beyond the generation of "pretty" images toward a medium capable of understanding and expressing complex human experience. Project page: https://github.com/songrise/SemJudge

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Interacting with Alexa: A Longitudinal Case Study of Voice Assistant Use in Down Syndrome
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As life expectancy for individuals with Down syndrome (DS) continues to increase, supporting cog- nitive engagement, everyday autonomy, and participation throughout adulthood has become an important research priority. Conversational voice assistants have emerged as promising assistive tech- nologies for these purposes, yet evidence regarding their long-term use in naturalistic settings remains limited. This paper presents a longitudinal case study of the everyday use of Amazon Alexa by an adult with Down syndrome over nine months in a real domestic environment. The study combines analyses of interaction logs, audio recordings, and qualitative observations to investigate usage pat- terns, interaction performance, communicative adaptation, and the integration of the voice assistant into everyday life. Results show that Alexa became progressively embedded in daily routines, sup- porting entertainment, information access, and autonomy-related activities. Longitudinal analyses reveal stable interaction patterns, reduced retry behavior, and the emergence of effective communi- cation strategies, while qualitative observations highlight increasing communicative engagement and the value of proactive reminders. The study also identifies important limitations of current commer- cial voice assistants, including reduced robustness to non-normative speech, limited conversational continuity, and poor contextual reasoning. Beyond providing rare ecologically valid evidence of long- term voice assistant use, the findings highlight design considerations that are relevant to the ongoing evolution of LLM-based conversational systems.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 19 pages, 16 figures, submitted to a Journal

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Can You Predict the Next Mind in the Symphony? Toward Multi-Turn Multi-Party Mental World Modeling
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Although multimodal foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in modeling, generation, and embodied reasoning in the physical world, their capacity for modeling the dynamic mental world remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on static mental state perception or single-turn behavioral reasoning, overlooking the dynamic mental transitions of the observed individuals in multi-party, multi-turn interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce M$^3$WME-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate mental world modeling conditioned on evolving actions of interactants. Specifically, models are tasked with forecasting a target subject's future mental states and behaviors over extended social interactions. In addition to the benchmark suite, we construct M$^3$WME-23K, a dedicated training dataset, and establish a competitive baseline named MindNext-7B. Extensive evaluations across four representative paradigms (general MLLMs, emotion-specialized MLLMs, agentic frameworks, and World Foundation Models) reveal that current systems consistently struggle to anticipate forward-looking mental states. Mechanistic analyses further reveal that existing architectures fundamentally lack forward mental state transition dynamics. Our findings highlight a pivotal challenge in advancing agents from physical to mental world modeling, charting new directions for socially adaptive AI.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Somatic Alignment: Scaffolding Non-Visible Inner Body Sensations in and beyond Vocal Pedagogy
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Inner bodily sensations inform expressive musical performance but can be difficult to interpret and communicate. Through two separate workshops with five singing learners and four senior voice teachers, we investigate breath control in vocal pedagogy. Participants reported difficulty interpreting bodily sensations (Opacity of Inner Sensations) and translating awareness into intended adjustments (Disconnected Regulation of Inner Sensations), alongside strategies involving touch, demonstration, and imagery. Building on these accounts, we propose the Somatic Alignment Model (SAM), connecting an Intrapersonal Self-Sensing Loop with an Intercorporeal Co-Sensing Loop. SAM examines how external guidance relates to learners' bodily calibration and how interpretive and regulatory authority is negotiated. We articulate three generative design dimensions, Modality, Agency, and Temporality, and illustrate their possible applications in interactive learning systems and first-person soma design inquiries. SAM offers a conceptual lens for supporting bodily awareness and regulation through interaction design.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MERIDIAN: Memory-Encoded Rituals for Intimacy across Distance in an Interactive, Asynchronous Neighbourhood
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: How can shared memories become playable structures for partners who live in different time zones, and what becomes of such a gift once it is in use? We present MERIDIAN, a design case of Yi Town, a bilingual browser game developed by one member of a long-distance couple as a gift for the other. Nine levels translate personally meaningful events, places and cultural references into tasks within a navigable pixel town, framed by a birthday prologue and a fictional wedding. This second version extends the record by four weeks. Drawing on research through design, we reconstruct seven design changes from 152 commits, 36 changelog versions and four design specifications. In those weeks the site gained three products that are not levels: an infirmary for the days after a quarrel, which began with a remark by the recipient; a page for her booked flight, which replaces a symbolic ticket with a real one; and a request box whose messages are answered, while the designer sleeps, by a pipeline of a local language model and a hosted one. The request box ends the first version's claim of no author-operated backend, and we trace where her files now travel. An audit reproduced 263 passing unit tests; the progress model is unchanged and keeps its exhaustive check of 1,024 codes. The answering pipeline was tested in parts, and it began to receive real requests on the night it was built. No recipient evaluation or relationship outcome is reported. The contribution is an inspectable account of design decisions and their trade-offs: between authoring a gift and leaving the recipient free to decline or reshape it, and between being reachable across thirteen hours and answering in person. The site is at https://jingyifan.love and its source is public at https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 27 pages, 25 figures, 11 tables. v2 adds four weeks of record and describes the dashboard, three further products, server, automated answering pipeline, service worker, and pose-analysis program. It corrects the backend claim and updates the audit. See "Changes in Version 2". Design case with no recipient evaluation reported

Human-Computer Interaction.title: GlassGround: GUI Grounding Beyond Native Screenshots with Egocentric Wearable Vision
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Wearable assistants must localize interface elements from camera observations when direct screenshot access is unavailable, yet existing GUI grounding benchmarks primarily evaluate native screenshots. We introduce GlassGround, a new benchmark that pairs native screenshots with wearable camera observations while holding GUI states, instructions, and targets fixed. GlassGround contains 3,250 tasks across Android and iOS, captured using four wearable devices under four viewing conditions. Across ten open-source models, mean grounding accuracy drops from 94.8% on screenshots to 48.5% on camera images. Further analysis reveals that changes in target scale, screen geometry, and background cannot fully explain this performance degradation. We then study two ways to narrow this gap. At inference time, local zooming and screen rectification help but leave most of the gap. For training-time adaptation, we build on GlassGround's paired-view design and introduce PairDistill, a baseline that aligns target representations across views alongside coordinate supervision. Trained on independently collected data and using no screenshots at inference, it improves camera-image accuracy by 9.4 and 12.2 points on two backbones and transfers to unseen devices and operating systems. Combined with local zooming, it reaches 69.6% and 64.4%, but does not close the gap. The GlassGround dataset and code are available at https://github.com/yunnw/GlassGround.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI Persona Dialogue Pipeline; From Survey Report to Conversational Personas, Evaluated by LLMs and Experts
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Simulating dialogue of a population with LLM-enacted personas is increasingly common, yet each pipeline is generally built for one task, so a new task usually means reworking how the persona is authored, enacted and evaluated. We present an end-to-end persona dialogue pipeline meant to carry over to other populations as a whole; a background is written by an LLM from a national survey report, an off-the-shelf LLM enacts it without fine-tuning, and both are rated for perceived plausibility. We apply it to thirty personas of Korean older adults living alone; three LLM judges compare eight simulator LLMs, and thirty experts who work with this population evaluate the selected one, GPT-5.5. Experts found the backgrounds and dialogues largely realistic but most often faulted a persona for being more capable than its background said, and agreement between their ratings and the LLM judges could not be established. We release the pipeline, personas and their dialogues.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: RoboJackVR: Turning Robot Tasks into VR Games for Scalable Demonstration Collection
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection systems that accommodate more participants and diverse tasks, yet teleoperation barriers and task-adaptation effort limit this expansion. We present RoboJackVR, a standalone virtual reality (VR) game in which players manipulate simulated robots to execute combat skills and contribute demonstrations. MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording run locally on the headset, removing the need for an external PC or simulation server during collection. Tutorials, skill selection, combat consequences, and character progression organize repeated task attempts within a continuing game. Task contracts declare assets, controls, resets, success criteria, and recording semantics; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect these declarations to task execution, outcome handling, and recording, allowing tasks to reuse the game flow while retaining their control and success semantics. Batch tools package supported resources and generate configurations, with manual adaptation and review for new interfaces and unsupported predicates. We instantiate the approach with SO101-Nexus-derived and LIBERO tasks. On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91% of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline's success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Knocking on Minds Door; A Mixed-Methods Field Study of a Voice LLM Companion in Older Adults Daily Lives
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Global aging makes digital technology important for older adults healthy aging, yet graphical user interfaces remain inaccessible to many. Voice agents based on large language models may help, but users needs and reasons for sustained use remain unclear. We developed a phone-call-style companion that initiates conversations proactively and structures calls using a persona, conversation rules, and prior-call memory (facts, insights, relationship background). We conducted a two-week mixed-methods field study with 33 community-dwelling Korean older adults (29 women; aged 67-91), collecting call logs, pre-post questionnaires, and interviews. Participants made 608 calls following a daily-use recommendation; 25 continued afterward despite turn-taking difficulties. Loneliness and depression scores decreased significantly; among loneliness subfactors, only isolation (emotional loneliness) decreased significantly. Participants disclosed concerns withheld from family and linked companionship to being addressed by name, being remembered, and experiencing emotional reciprocity. We propose personalized conversation rules, accessible interaction, and user control over frequency and topics.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for medical education, but most existing systems focus on localized interactions such as question answering or single-turn feedback, rather than organizing an entire clinical case into a decision-centered learning trajectory. We introduce \textit{MedGame}, a framework that transforms static clinical cases into structured, executable storytelling games. MedGame uses a dual-engine design: a Medical Narrative Designer synthesizes case-grounded clinical storylines with states and decision nodes, while a Story Director converts them into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans rendered by our released interactive platform. We construct MedGame Bench, a 5,000-case benchmark and evaluation protocol for Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction. Experiments show that task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves open-source LLMs on MedGame Bench and narrows the gap with commercial models. A pilot student study further shows that learners perceive MedGame as more engaging and useful than text-only alternatives.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Work in Progress; an explorational design and study on AI+Education+Game. Updated an author's affiliation. A further revision (v3) is in preparation

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Before They Were Cool: Do Early Fans Abandon Artists Who Suddenly Become Popular? Evidence from Online Music Listening
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Identity-signalling theory, echoed in the hipster's "I liked them before they were cool", expects an artist's first fans to pull away once the artist becomes popular, by leaving or by avoiding what the newcomers play. A rival account expects the event that brings the crowd to renew existing listeners' attention to the artist. We test both in the Last.fm listening histories of 594,415 users (21.1 billion plays, 2005-2013), where every play appears on the user's profile. Study 1 detects 78 crowd arrivals: months in which the number of people discovering an artist tripled without a new album, single or EP, for example after a song appeared in a film. Study 2 compares Grammy and Mercury Prize winners with nominees who won nothing. We compare listeners who had played the artist before the crowd arrived (early fans) with early fans of comparison artists. Early fans did not withdraw. Those still listening stopped less often (25.8% vs. 29.1% over six months), and those who had drifted away returned more often (29.6% vs. 25.0%). Those who kept listening converged on the crowd: the song most newcomers played took a larger share of their plays, with no turn to deep cuts. More lapsed fans returned after larger surges, and neither fans with the most distinctive tastes nor fans facing a more mainstream crowd quit more. Award wins brought few new listeners and no clear change. Where listening is displayed by default, early fans moved towards the crowd after sudden popularity, not away from it.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Evaluating Strategies for Multimodal Bidirectional Interactions between Pedestrians and AVs
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) share spaces with Vulnerable Road Users (VRUs) in encounters where driver cues are absent. This can leave people uncertain whether the vehicle has noticed them and understood their request. Existing research has studied how AVs communicate with pedestrians through external human-machine interfaces. This work investigates bidirectional multimodal VRU-AV interactions combining Augmented Reality (AR), speech, and gestures. The study follows four stages: literature synthesis of interactions, a survey with 124 participants, interaction loop implementation, and feasibility evaluation. Participants preferred AR cues that made vehicle motion or warnings explicit, high-level voice commands, and conventional gestures. Prototype measurements revealed a trade-off between faster local processing and more accurate infrastructure-assisted processing. The demonstration shows bidirectional interaction using AR wearables and vehicular communications, while leaving decision-making to the AV. Together, the results support treating AV-VRU interaction as a closed loop of intent expression, recognition, vehicle decision, and feedback.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EgoCARBS: Egocentric Video Meets Active Acoustics for Kitchen Action Understanding
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Egocentric video records what a person looks at, but often misses what their body does: the hands leave the frame, and arm motion goes unseen. An exocentric camera recovers this context, but it must be installed wherever the activity happens. Active acoustic sensing can recover it from the wearables themselves: a device's speaker emits inaudible chirps, and its microphone senses the motion of the hands, arms, and nearby objects from their echoes. Yet no public dataset pairs it with egocentric video. We present EgoCARBS, with two deliverables. The first is a multimodal dataset and benchmark: 15 participants cook unscripted meals in their own kitchens wearing camera glasses and an off-the-shelf smartwatch that both sense with active acoustics, synchronized with egocentric and exocentric video and the watch's audio and IMU, with 4,019 verb-noun action annotations in 11.4 hours. The second is a study of what the wearables add to egocentric video. On verb recognition, they add at least as much as an exocentric camera for participants seen in training, and even more for new participants, for whom the exocentric camera does not help. Active acoustics alone provides most of this gain, and helps most where the camera does not see the hands. Trimmed action recognition, detection, and anticipation remain open. We will release the data, our data collection and annotation tools, and pre-trained models.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 36 pages (12 main paper and references, 24 supplementary material). Project page: https://saif-mahmud.github.io/projects/ego-carbs

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Designing human and generative AI collaboration: Trade-offs in productivity, satisfaction, and creative diversity
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Rapid advances in generative AI have raised hopes for major productivity gains but recent research has also raised concerns about declining worker satisfaction and reduced creative diversity. While prior research has documented each of these effects individually, it remains unclear how collaboration design shapes the costs that accompany AI-enabled productivity gains. We address this question through a human-subjects experiment on a 1,000-word creative writing task, comparing three human-AI collaboration designs. Completion time was similar across the three designs but quality, satisfaction, and diversity differed across them. The Human Confirmation design, in which AI led ideation, outlining, drafting, and editing while humans primarily confirmed or rejected output, showed the clearest downsides: lower quality and satisfaction, and lower aggregate genre and semantic diversity. By contrast, designs that preserved human involvement in preproduction or throughout the writing process avoided the clearest quality and satisfaction losses without requiring longer overall completion times. Preserving active human involvement in preproduction was also associated with lower aggregate similarity in content than Human Confirmation. These findings show that collaboration design substantially reshapes trade-offs between efficiency, quality, satisfaction, and diversity, suggesting that the central challenge is not whether to adopt AI, but how to allocate creative control between humans and AI. That choice shapes not only the output of creative work but the experience of creative agency.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Published in PNAS Nexus 5(11), pgag353 (2026). Supplementary Information is available with the published article at https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag353

Machine Learning.title: Tokenisation is not in APX
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.

Machine Learning.title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
Machine Learning.summary: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.

Machine Learning.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
Machine Learning.summary:
AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong.
  The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

Machine Learning.title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models
Machine Learning.summary: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.

Machine Learning.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
Machine Learning.summary: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

Machine Learning.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
Machine Learning.summary: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT

Machine Learning.title: Point2SSM++: Self-Supervised Learning of Anatomical Shape Models from Point Clouds
Machine Learning.summary: Correspondence-based statistical shape modeling (SSM) stands as a powerful technology for morphometric analysis in clinical research. SSM facilitates population-level characterization and quantification of anatomical shapes such as bones and organs, aiding in pathology and disease diagnostics and treatment planning. Despite its potential, SSM remains under-utilized in medical research due to the significant overhead associated with automatic construction methods, which demand complete, aligned shape surface representations. Additionally, optimization-based techniques rely on bias-inducing assumptions or templates and have prolonged inference times as the entire cohort is simultaneously optimized. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Point2SSM++, a principled, self-supervised deep learning approach that directly learns correspondence points from point cloud representations of anatomical shapes. Point2SSM++ is robust to misaligned and inconsistent input, providing SSM that accurately samples individual shape surfaces while effectively capturing population-level statistics. Furthermore, we present extensions of Point2SSM++ tailored for dynamic spatiotemporal and multi-anatomy scenarios, showcasing the broad versatility of the framework.
