  However, held-out review comments and hidden-test resolution did not improve after ten retrospectives. Tracing each step of the loop, we found that sparse review signal (0.45 comments/PR) left little to learn from and that rules admitted on their stated evidence did not show measurable held-out effects. We derive six lessons and argue that governed loops should admit and retire every learned rule as a testable hypothesis.
Software Engineering.comment: 5 pages, 2 figures

Software Engineering.title: ReqSeek: Transformer-Based Automatic Requirements Identification for Building Large Requirements Datasets
Software Engineering.summary: Large, diverse, and high-quality datasets are significant for advancing AI in requirements engineering, yet automated identification of requirements from Software Requirement Specifications (SRS) remains a challenge. Automatic Requirements Identification (ARI) methods demonstrate limited generalization to unseen documents across heterogeneous SRSs. This work presents ReqSeek, a transformer-based, domain-agnostic ARI model for recognizing ISO 29148-style requirements in SRS documents, supporting dataset construction. We curated the Automatic Requirements Identification Dataset (ARID), comprising 2,396 training instances from 23 heterogeneous SRSs, and fine-tuned four transformer architectures. RoBERTa was selected as the base model for ReqSeek and achieved 95% precision, recall, F1, and F0.89 on the held-out evaluation set. Exploratory human-model benchmarking showed performance comparable to humans while requiring substantially less prediction time than manual annotation. Post-hoc evaluation on out-of-domain (OoD) SRSs provided evidence of requirement identification beyond ARID. Robustness analysis demonstrated ReqSeek's insensitivity to minor linguistic variations while maintaining sensitivity to major ISO 29148-style violations. We applied ReqSeek to construct the Software Requirements Dataset (SwaRD), identifying 10,201 ISO 29148-style requirements from 231 industrial SRSs. SwaRD aligns with textual and semantic properties of human-curated datasets while exceeding them in scale and domain diversity. Our results suggest that transformer-based ARI can provide precise and generalizable requirements identification.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM), 2026

Software Engineering.title: AutoRPG: Harnessing Systematic AI for Non-Intrusive Low-Latency Mobile RPG Combat
Software Engineering.summary: Automated combat in mobile RPGs plays a critical role in game quality assurance, requiring real-time behavior control that closely resembles human gameplay. However, existing approaches fail to satisfy these requirements, either because they lack fine-grained behavioral control or because they incur high inference latency. To address these challenges, we incorporate user gameplay experience to design AutoRPG, a systematic AI framework for automating mobile RPG combat. At a high level, AutoRPG decomposes the combat process into two stages: a high-level strategic planning phase that formulates the overall combat strategy, followed by a systematic execution phase powered by a suite of carefully designed lightweight modules encompassing target tracking, character movement, dodge maneuvering, and abnormal-state handling. Experiments on three popular mobile RPGs, i.e., Genshin Impact, Wuthering Waves, and Arknights: Endfield, demonstrate that AutoRPG consistently outperforms four competitive baselines across both combat quality and generalization capability, while behaving the most similarly to human players among all evaluated agents.

Software Engineering.title: fx(hash): Salvaging The Source Code of 28k Generative Artworks
Software Engineering.summary: fx(hash), the most radically inclusive generative art NFT platform, went bankrupt and shut down on August 17, 2026. The ownership of its 2,705,350 artworks is immutable on the Tezos and Ethereum blockchains, but the source code that generates them is off-chain and in peril. We salvaged all 28,193 generative programs contributed by 5,532 international artists and archived them in Software Heritage. Here we explain why NFT generative art is fragile and the steps we took to salvage these software cultural landmarks.

Software Engineering.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
Software Engineering.summary: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
Software Engineering.comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables. Project page: https://cmu-l3.github.io/kernel-shift/

Software Engineering.title: Agentic Harness Engineering: Observability-Driven Automatic Evolution of Coding-Agent Harnesses
Software Engineering.summary: Harnesses are now central to coding-agent performance, mediating how models interact with tools and execution environments. Yet harness engineering remains a manual craft, because automating it faces a heterogeneous action space across editable components, voluminous trajectories that bury actionable signal, and edits whose effect is hard to attribute. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering (AHE), a closed loop that addresses these challenges through three matched observability pillars: (1) component observability gives every editable harness component a file-level representation so the action space is explicit and revertible; (2) experience observability distills millions of raw trajectory tokens into a layered, drill-down evidence corpus that an evolving agent can actually consume; and (3) decision observability pairs every edit with a self-declared prediction, later verified against the next round's task-level outcomes. Together, these pillars turn every edit into a falsifiable contract, so harness evolution proceeds autonomously without collapsing into trial-and-error. Empirically, ten AHE iterations lift pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2 from 69.7% to 77.0%, surpassing the human-designed harness Codex-CLI (71.9%) and the self-evolving baselines ACE and TF-GRPO. The frozen harness transfers without re-evolution: on SWE-bench-verified it tops aggregate success at 12% fewer tokens than the seed, and on Terminal-Bench 2 it yields +5.1 to +10.1pp cross-family gains across three alternate model families, indicating the evolved components encode general engineering experience rather than benchmark-specific tuning. Ablations localize the gain to tools, middleware, and long-term memory rather than the system prompt, suggesting factual harness structure transfers while prose-level strategy does not.

Software Engineering.title: MARGIN: Margin-Aware Regularized Geometry for Imbalanced Vulnerability Detection
Software Engineering.summary: Software vulnerability detection is critical for ensuring software security and reliability. Despite recent advances in deep learning, real-world vulnerability datasets suffer from two severe challenges: frequency imbalance and difficulty imbalance. We reinterpret these challenges from an embedding geometry perspective, observing that such imbalances induce geometric distortions in hyperspherical representation space. To address this issue, we propose MARGIN, a metric-based framework that learns discriminative vulnerability representations through adaptive margin metric learning and hyperspherical prototype modeling. MARGIN dynamically adjusts geometric regularization according to the distribution structure estimated by the von Mises-Fisher concentration, aligning the probability mass of embedding distributions with their corresponding Voronoi cells, thereby reducing geometric distortion and yielding more stable decision boundaries. Extensive experiments on public vulnerability datasets show that MARGIN consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving notable improvements in classification and detection, especially on challenging, imbalanced datasets. Further analysis demonstrates that MARGIN produces more structured embedding geometries, improving robustness, interpretability, and generalization.
Software Engineering.comment: 29 pages.10 figures, 6 tables

Software Engineering.title: Endpoint-Conditioned Process Value: What an Endpoint-Blind Process Score Adds Once Terminal Status and Cost Are Known
Software Engineering.summary: Trajectory metrics promise information beyond final-answer accuracy, but no one has measured what a process score adds once an evaluation knows the outcome and the cost. We build that comparison: a sealed consequence needing an artifact neither agent nor judge ever sees, an operational baseline of terminal status and cost, and judge scale and evidence access as experimental factors. On 1,255 trajectories over 158 test-generation tasks in 7 Python repositories, the answer is gated on the judge. Four judges from 4B to 14B, one reasoning before scoring, add nothing an interval separates from zero; a Qwen3 32B judge on identical trajectories adds +0.050 AUC (95% CI [+0.020, +0.081]) and survives a refitting bootstrap ([+0.013, +0.095]). Most of what it adds is recoverable from eight behavioural counters, so a harness should log them (the judge adds +0.020 beyond them). What the judge is shown moves it further: disclosing the terminal verdict inflates its standalone discrimination by +0.103, while reference disclosure and tool-output redaction move it by nothing an interval separates from zero. A process metric reported without the judge's scale and evidence access does not identify a quantity. We release the protocol, the sealed-endpoint harness, and all trajectories.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted by EACL

Software Engineering.title: Looking Is Not Picking: An Attention-Segment Account of Tool-Selection Failures in LLM Agents
Software Engineering.summary: LLM agents mis-call tools, and the natural guess is that the model failed to see the right tool in a crowded harness. We show the opposite through a lens concurrent work sets aside -- the model's attention to labeled tool-definition segments. On real BFCL failures, by per-candidate attention argmax the model attends most to the correct tool 80% of the time (vs. 21% chance), and the gold is the under-attended segment on only 10%: it looks at the right tool and still picks wrong. This directly refutes the intuitive "crowded-harness / lost-in-the-middle" explanation: the failure is at the decision readout, not the harness, and we pin it there three ways. (1) Input vs. readout: repairing the prompt (reordering or duplicating the gold tool) recovers <=23% of failures, while readout-side interventions recover 59-91%. (2) Representation-invariance: two gold-pointed interventions in different representations -- an additive attention-logit bias and a residual-stream steering vector -- recover largely the same failures (per-task Jaccard 0.865 pooled, 0.79-0.91 per model), so the bottleneck is localized to the readout independent of which representation is poked. (3) A training-free, gold-free selector: per-segment attention closes most of the gold-free-vs-oracle gap on BFCL (+11.9 pts pooled function-name selection vs. +17.9-pt oracle headroom) and adds +14.9 pts on Seal-Tools; every model positive (exact McNemar p<=8e-4 each). Scopes differ: the causal attention-bias dose-response is bidirectional and monotonic on 10 mask-honoring models (3-32B), the full 0.5-32B span carrying only the correlational diagnostic; the deployable selector is evaluated on 5 single-turn models and does not yet transfer to a multi-turn loop.
Software Engineering.comment: This submission is withdrawn by the author. Upon re-evaluation, I find the experimental design and validation in this version lack sufficient rigor, and the overall work does not meet the expected standard. I will conduct more careful experiments, strengthen the analysis, and submit a thoroughly revised manuscript when ready

Software Engineering.title: DynaFix: Iterative Automated Program Repair Driven by Execution-Level Dynamic Information
Software Engineering.summary: Automated Program Repair (APR) seeks to generate correct patches for buggy programs, but recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based repair systems remain sensitive to superficial code changes and often rely on coarse test outcomes during iterative repair. We propose DynaFix, an LLM-based APR framework that integrates execution-level dynamic information into a closed-loop repair workflow. The distinguishing feature of DynaFix lies not in using execution-level information per se, but in repeatedly updating and exploiting such information throughout the iterative repair process. In each repair round, DynaFix uses ByteTrace to collect variable states, branch paths, and call stacks, incorporates these runtime signals into structured prompts, validates generated patches through re-execution, and feeds the resulting updated traces into subsequent repair iterations. This process grounds patch generation in concrete execution behavior rather than static code alone. We evaluate DynaFix on Defects4J v2.0, the Real-World Benchmark, and a code perturbation benchmark, Defects4J-Trans. DynaFix repairs 236 single-function Defects4J bugs with GPT-4 and 186 with GPT-4o, including 23 bugs not fixed by existing baselines. On Defects4J-Trans, DynaFix achieves 15.6%-32.1% higher aggregate repair counts than ReinFix and shows higher repair retention under semantics-preserving transformations. It also reduces token consumption by 60%-70% compared with state-of-the-art LLM-based APR methods. These results show that repeatedly updating and exploiting execution-level information throughout iterative repair can substantially improve the effectiveness, robustness, and cost efficiency of LLM-based program repair.
Software Engineering.comment: 34 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in Journal of Systems and Software

Software Engineering.title: MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.
Software Engineering.comment: 16 pages, including appendices. The MetaSkill library is provided as ancillary material

Software Engineering.title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation (Extended Version)
Software Engineering.summary: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted to POPL '27; Extended version with appendices

Software Engineering.title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.

Software Engineering.title: SatMend: LLM Agents for Automated Software Repair in Satellite Constellations with Intermittent Ground Contact
Software Engineering.summary: Satellite constellations rely on onboard software to sustain services across cooperating spacecraft. Maintaining this software requires handling related component versions and different failure causes while delivering repairs through intermittent ground contact. Automated software repair in satellite constellations remains underexplored, particularly the coordination of repairs across related versions with verified onboard recovery under intermittent ground contact. To address this gap, we propose SatMend, a software repair method driven by ground-based large language model (LLM) agents. SatMend organizes related versions into persistent sessions to retain diagnostic context and combines source and runtime evidence to select code repair or state recovery actions. It validates each version separately and submits ready candidates during continued repair, allowing ground preparation to overlap with onboard delivery and verification. Experimental results show that across configurations with 16 to 64 satellites, SatMend restores 192 of 224 faulty applications within 600 s, compared with 40 for SWE-agent, 77 for Agentless, 124 for RepairAgent, and 115 for SWE-Search. These results demonstrate SatMend's effectiveness in restoring applications and supporting service continuity in satellite constellations with intermittent ground contact.

Software Engineering.title: Implementation and Software-in-the-Loop Evaluation of a Trans-Domain Digital Twin Architecture for Autonomous Guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV Without Online GNSS
Software Engineering.summary: Autonomous UAV guidance in emergency response, infrastructure monitoring, and cargo transportation requires reliable navigation. However, satellite-based positioning may become unavailable or unreliable in enclosed spaces, blind spots caused by natural obstacles and structures, and environments affected by radio interference and signal spoofing during electronic warfare. This study designs, implements, and evaluates a system based on a Trans-Domain Digital Twin (TDDT) for autonomous guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV. Independent navigation, flight dynamics, and meteorological models are coordinated within a cycle of state estimation, prediction, decision-making, command execution, and feedback. Data from inertial, magnetic, pressure, and airspeed sensors, together with environmental information, form the basis for estimation and prediction. Furthermore, a shared state, temporal synchronization, preservation of information provenance, and command traceability establish continuity between models and decisions. The system was tested with a simulated physical twin in a software-in-the-loop environment. Vertical takeoff, movement toward the destination, landing, and autonomous stopping were recorded, and the dynamic model was adjusted to a limited extent based on sensor-derived feedback. Separating the evaluation reference from navigation inputs enabled independent assessment of positioning error and computational performance. The results confirm operational coordination, decision traceability, and closed-loop guidance under the tested conditions, providing a reproducible platform for the development and evaluation of navigation without satellite-based positioning.
Software Engineering.comment: 34 pages, 17 figures, 4 tables. Software-in-the-loop evaluation of GNSS-independent Phoenix VTOL guidance using a trans-domain digital twin architecture. Source code and reproducibility materials: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24419538

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Event-Time Confounding Under Bursty Human Dynamics
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Web studies often measure what happens after a user action, such as a search after a chatbot answer. To credit an AI answer with later commercial activity, a study must separate what the answer caused from what the user would have done anyway. But people act in the middle of activity already underway, so the activity that drives what follows also chooses when the clock starts. We call this endogenous time zero. Using an opt-in panel that links conversational-AI use, browsing, and search, we insert inert timestamps (moments that match recent activity but mark no event) and rerun the standard analysis. In a pre-registered replication, these timestamps, which by construction cannot cause anything, reproduce 76% of the search increase after AI responses that follow recent browsing. Other users matched on 30-day activity, the usual control, give the same answer, and inert timestamps show a similar search excess across 16 kinds of Web events. Comparing with moments of matching recent history removes most of the increase, but no placebo audit we ran could confirm that this comparison is unbiased, and published studies almost never run one. We give a protocol for choosing comparisons and stress-testing estimators.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: v2: shortened and refocused version (inert-timestamp placebo test for user-timed Web events, a sweep across event types, reference-moment comparisons, and a protocol); 12 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: after recommending answers, 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing.
  We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Managing Uncertainty in Teacher Vibe Coding: A Comparison of Teacher and Expert Workflows
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Vibe coding, or natural language software development, enables teachers to become creators of digital teaching artifacts. However, novice educators oftentimes face different barriers. This qualitative study examined the workflows of pre-service teachers, in-service teachers, and expert developers through think-aloud protocols. Findings reveal vibe coding operates through a loop of problem framing, development, and verification governed by uncertainty management. Teachers reduced uncertainty by grounding designs in authentic needs: pre-service teachers drew on pedagogical principles, whereas in-service teachers relied on everyday teaching challenges. Conversely, Experts reduced ambiguity by constraining requirements, decomposing artifacts into testable modules, and automating tests. These differences reveal complementary forms of pedagogical, contextual, and technical expertise. Future work may be about supporting nontechnical teachers in developing reliable and educational applications.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Accepted for presentation at the 2027 American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting

Human-Computer Interaction.title: But Can You Draw It Live? The Emergence of AI Duidus for Adjudicating Suspected Generative AI Use in Digital Art Commission Communities
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI poses new challenges for digital art commission communities, where a commission's value often depends on human labor and authorship. We examine a novel community-developed dispute resolution mechanism called an AI duidu, or livestreamed drawing bet, used when an artist is suspected of using generative AI. In an AI duidu, an accuser challenges an artist to create a new artwork live, and community members vote on whether the artist created the disputed artwork without AI assistance. Often, both parties stake money with an intermediary, who releases it after the vote. Through interviews with 17 accusers, accused artists, or intermediaries, we examined how the AI duidu emerged and how participants perceived its effectiveness and risks. We found that AI duidus shift authorship verification from the artwork itself to the artist, using livestreamed creative labor, community adjudication, and wagering to establish provenance and negotiate community norms surrounding AI use.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Immersive Video Effects Persist Beyond Exposure: From Psychological Closeness to Self-Initiated Behaviour in a Two-Week Comparison with 2D Video
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Immersive Video (IV), a live-action stereoscopic 180-degree video format, has been shown to elicit a strong sense of Presence and enhance psychological closeness to individuals depicted in the video. However, whether these effects persist beyond exposure and are accompanied by subsequent self-initiated behaviour remains unclear. In this study, 84 participants were assigned to either an IV or a 2D video group, and psychological and behavioural outcomes were tracked over a two-week period. Psychological outcomes were assessed before and immediately after exposure and at approximately 3, 7, and 14 days post-exposure, while self-initiated behaviour was assessed during follow-up. Psychological closeness remained significantly higher in the IV group than in the 2D group for up to 7 days and remained elevated above baseline within the IV group at 14 days. Lasting-impression ratings were also significantly higher in the IV group throughout the follow-up period. Among participants who completed both scheduled follow-up assessments, 45.9% in the IV group met the operational criterion for early self-initiated engagement, compared with 13.2% in the 2D group. Furthermore, a higher proportion of participants in the IV group reported active or socially oriented behaviours. These findings suggest that IV can elicit psychological effects that persist beyond exposure and may encourage subsequent self-initiated engagement.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: LLM Support for Mathematical Problem Posing: What Changes When Revision Formulations Are Supplied or Withheld?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In mathematical problem posing, participants construct or modify problems rather than only solve predefined ones, creating opportunities for Large Language Models (LLMs) to support how those problems are formulated and revised. We investigate two forms of LLM support for revising participant-generated problems: Socratic scaffolding, which uses guiding questions while withholding candidate formulations, and Direct scaffolding, which provides concrete alternative formulations. We conducted a counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 graduate students who posed and revised problems across two mathematical scenarios. Problems showed larger immediate supported artifact-quality gains under Direct than Socratic scaffolding. Exploratory dimension-level analyses identified statistically significant differences in structural clarity and novelty after correction for multiple comparisons. Socratic scaffolding was associated with longer revision time, highlighting a contrast between immediate artifact outcomes and revision processes. These findings identify the amount of candidate revision content supplied by an LLM as an important design variable in mathematical problem posing.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Micro-level AI Feedback Features and Student Responses in Consecutive LLM Tutoring Interactions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI-assisted feedback research has shown that micro-level feedback features, such as concrete elaboration, affective language, and response length, are associated with learning outcomes. Existing studies have primarily examined these features using session- or task-level measures. We examine how feedback provided in one user-AI interaction is associated with student confusion and understanding in the immediately following interaction in a naturalistic tutoring setting. We focus on three micro-level features of AI feedback: concrete elaboration (analogies, comparison-based explanations, or worked examples), affective language (encouragement, empathy, or apology), and response length. We analyzed 16,851 conversational user-AI interactions from the StudyChat dataset, a naturalistic record of student interactions with an LLM tutor in an undergraduate AI course, and identified 1,718 cases in which students expressed confusion and continued to a subsequent interaction. Using chi-square tests and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE), we found that concrete elaboration was associated with higher understanding and lower re-confusion in the student's next interaction. Empathetic language showed no significant association with either outcome, while longer responses were independently associated with lower understanding. These findings highlight the value of examining feedback across consecutive user-AI interactions and suggest that concrete elaboration may play an important role in supporting immediate student understanding.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Unified Choice Model of News Selection: Experimental Evidence on Stance, Rank, and Engagement Cues
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Social media platforms often display visual engagement cues alongside ranked news articles, yet their influence on clicks remains poorly understood when considered jointly with ranking position and users' political preferences. We propose a unified discrete choice framework using a conditional multinomial logit model to jointly estimate and compare the influence of these factors on news selection. We evaluate the model using 1,480 choices from 370 human participants across four news topics in a controlled study with and without visual engagement cues. The framework allows us to assess the incremental contribution of each factor through nested-model likelihood-ratio tests. We find that including visual engagement cues significantly improves model fit across all topics after accounting for rank and stance. Engagement cues alone also predict clicks better than either of these features, although the full model achieves the highest held-out log-likelihood. Finally, we quantify via counterfactual analysis the impact of ranking position and displayed engagement counts on click probabilities. These findings can inform platform owners, researchers, and policymakers evaluating how platform design affects the selection of political news.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Managing Verification Debt: A Framework for Responsible Human-AI Research Partnerships
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Conversation with generative artificial intelligence (AI) can quickly turn a tentative scientific question into the outline of a research programme. Although this capability can accelerate research, it also places two closely related pressures on human intelligence: 1) temporal asymmetry between rapid AI generation and slower expert evaluation, and 2) a cognitive gap between the available effort, expertise, attention and capacity to assess AI outputs. When unexamined AI contributions are carried into subsequent claims or decisions, these pressures produce verification debt: validation work that remains outstanding before a contribution can be relied upon. If left unresolved, this debt can undermine responsible AI in research, understood here as the transparent and traceable use of AI under effective human oversight and accountability. This commentary argues that responsible human--AI research partnerships therefore require a disciplined method for managing verification debt, not better prompting alone. We propose a shared topology of the research programme: a structured representation that connects questions, claims, assumptions, sources, tests and decisions while recording their provenance, dependencies and verification status. The topology makes unresolved debt visible, enables corrections to propagate through dependent claims and requires consequential contributions to be examined at decision gates before research proceeds. We consider its application in two-way partnerships and supervised partnerships that extend from doctoral research to multi-way research teams, and examine its implications for scholarly assessment, peer review and empirical evaluation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Chameleon: Exploring Risk Interpretation through Scene-Matched Textures in Virtual Reality
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Users in virtual reality need to judge contact risks around physical objects while remaining engaged in the virtual scene. Scene-matched textures give physical objects a place in virtual reality and provide visual cues for interaction. We examine how Chameleon's risk-aware textures are perceived during a reaching task. A study with 42 participants compared scanned appearances with red warnings, uniform environment textures, and risk-aware scene-matched textures. Participants rated the risk-aware condition more favorably on four aspects of perceived cue clarity than both alternatives. Interviews connected visible warnings with initial caution and linked confidence in physical interaction to material expectations and intended actions. Awareness of an object's location did not necessarily imply confidence in interacting with it. These findings motivate risk cues that connect depicted materials to the physical properties relevant to an intended action, and ways to support verification during interaction.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

Human-Computer Interaction.title: ARRANGE: Agentic Skills for Layering Vocals
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Adding a singing voice to an existing piano recording requires decisions about melody, syllable placement, pronunciation, timing, and vocal register. ARRANGE organizes this work as a sequence of agent skills with readable intermediate artifacts and composer approval checkpoints. An LLM translates instructions in plain English, notes played on a keyboard, and vocal references into local edits; deterministic scripts validate and apply those edits before open audio models render the result. The Score Canvas makes note, syllable, and pronunciation decisions inspectable and editable. In a benchmark of 16 revision requests, three draws per request, and five LLMs, typed edits achieved exact-change correctness of 0.83-0.98, compared with 0.33-0.69 for whole-plan rewriting without ARRANGE instructions. A separate score-editing benchmark and a first-person worked example examine the interaction between representations and corrections. Author listening evaluations further explore voice transfer and register selection, including 185 listening presentations across eight copied voices. These evaluations support the value of constrained editing and expose limits of both model execution and listening measures. The contribution is an interaction architecture for retaining musical decisions through inspectable intermediate representations, rather than a new singing model or evidence of general usability.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Under review at the HUMANE-LLM workshop, ACM IUI 2027 (Helsinki). Code: https://github.com/htansetiawan/ARRANGE ; project page: https://htansetiawan.github.io/ARRANGE

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Play and Learn: Gamified Feedback for Ultrasound-Guided Catheter Insertion Training in Virtual Reality
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: VR is widely used in procedural medical training, but many simulators prioritize realism over formative feedback. We developed a gamified VR simulator for ultrasound-guided peripheral IV catheter insertion, using aligned visual and auditory feedback such as progress indicators, guidance, and rewards. In studies with novices (N=24) and clinicians (N=12), gamification reduced task time, improved usability, and lowered workload. Qualitative results showed clearer goals and greater confidence for novices, and improved pacing for experts. Overall, gamification can provide effective formative feedback in VR medical training.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EVis+: Literature-Grounded Visual Analytics for Hypothesis-Driven Geoscientific Data Exploration
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Scientific researchers often interpret observational data in light of prior findings reported in the scientific literature. However, scientific literature typically remains external to visual analytics environments, requiring researchers to manually connect published findings with the data and hypotheses under investigation. In this paper, we present EVis+, a literature-grounded visual analytics system for condition-event time series analysis in geoscience. EVis+ enhances observational data exploration by retrieving and synthesizing literature-derived insights relevant to the dataset and analytical goals, transforming user-selected insights into testable hypotheses and mapping them to domain-specific visualizations through expert-curated templates, and supporting evidence examination, discrepancy validation, and literature-driven re-exploration to support iterative hypothesis refinement and scientific exploration. Rather than handing scientific analysis to an unconstrained language model, EVis+ uses structured AI-assisted transformations that keep intermediate results visible, allowing researchers to inspect and guide the analysis at each step. We evaluate the system through an evidence-grounding audit, a structured expert assessment of the insights, and case studies with geoscientists and a comparative study with domain experts.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: DataRecycle: Trustworthy Distillation of Structured Data from Scattered Web Evidence
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The web contains vast amounts of scattered quantitative evidence that is difficult to organize into comparable and verifiable structures. Yet its unstructured, sparse, and sometimes conflicting nature makes a systematic distillation costly and error-prone. Existing approaches force users to make a trade-off: search engines return document lists that require labor-intensive extraction and reconciliation, while generative AI systems produce fluent summaries that obscure data provenance, introduce reporting bias, and hide inconsistencies. We present DataRecycle, an interactive system that helps transform scattered web evidence into structured tables of comparable numerical facts. Given a user's query or statement, DataRecycle decomposes it into entities and attributes, retrieves candidate evidence, and organizes scattered, potentially conflicting records in a table-based evidence view. To address key challenges in automated data distillation (i.e., incomplete retrieval, untraceable generation, sparse data distribution, and multi-source inconsistency), DataRecycle adopts an ontology-guided, top-down data acquisition strategy, visualizes the recorded lineage from retrieved snippets to extracted values, and aligns heterogeneous data across dimensions such as time, definition, and scale. We evaluate DataRecycle through module-level experiments, a usage scenario, and a user study, showing that the system helps users organize numerical web evidence into provenance-linked tables and inspect uncertainty and conflicting sources.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation via Topology-Aware Distillation and Progressive Kinematic Reasoning
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Hand pose estimation aims to recover the spatial configuration of hand joints from visual observations and serves as a fundamental perception module for downstream systems that rely on complete and topologically consistent hand representations. Most existing methods are developed under the assumption of fully articulated hand structures and tend to produce unstable or implausible predictions when parts of the kinematic structure are persistently absent, resulting in degraded performance or even system failure despite available partial observations. To study this challenge, we construct IncNYU, a physiologically constrained benchmark that simulates structural incompleteness through morphological modification of complete hand models and retains reference locations for both intact and synthetically removed regions. Based on this benchmark, we propose InsHaPE, an Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation framework designed to remain robust under structural incompleteness while preserving performance on standard, fully articulated hands. Built on hierarchical kinematic modeling, InsHaPE introduces two complementary components. First, a topology-aware distillation strategy transfers joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hand representations, providing anatomically consistent initialization under missing structures. Second, a progressive kinematic reasoning module performs structured inference along the kinematic chain, enabling complete and anatomically consistent pose estimation under severe structural variations. Extensive experiments on NYU/IncNYU, together with external validation on MSRA, demonstrate that InsHaPE improves robustness under structural incompleteness while maintaining competitive performance on complete hands. System-level evaluations further show that InsHaPE improves robustness for downstream applications that require fixed-topology hand pose representations.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

Software Engineering.title: Operational Runbooks as Living Documents: A Longitudinal Study of Document Evolution under Assisted Post-Incident Revision
Software Engineering.summary: Operational runbooks increasingly function as living documents within operational workflows: they are maintained by people, used in incident support, and continuously revised as organizational knowledge changes. Yet little is known about how such document collections evolve over time in production settings, or which interpretable signals are useful for monitoring document change. We analyze 17 weeks of version-controlled runbook snapshots produced during post-incident revision with machine-assisted review and human oversight. We quantify document evolution using lightweight linguistic and structural signals grounded in prior work on procedural language, technical communication, and document organization. Correlation analysis shows mixed patterns of association, including both positive and negative relationships, with effect sizes ranging from negligible to moderate and varying across corpora. Temporal summaries further distinguish comparatively stable signals from revision-sensitive ones, supporting monitoring of document maintenance workflows rather than one-shot quality judgments. An illustrative analysis on public GitHub product documentation shows that signal behavior differs across corpora, reinforcing the need for context-aware interpretation. These results identify which metric classes provide stable anchors and which provide edit-sensitive indicators for managing operational documentation as an engineered document resource.
Software Engineering.comment: 11 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the 2026 ACM Symposium on Document Engineering (DocEng 2026). Includes appendices

Software Engineering.title: SWE-Pruner Pro: The Coder LLM Already Knows What to Prune
Software Engineering.summary: Pruning long context for coding agents has been a vital technology for efficient context management. While existing context pruning methods such as SWE-Pruner realize this by attaching a separate code classifier, we find the agent itself encodes internal representations indicating the relevance of code context when reading tool output. Based on this finding, we propose SWE-Pruner Pro, which prunes tool outputs directly inside the agent. Concretely, a small head turns the agent's own internal representations into a keep-or-prune label for each line, with a length-aware embedding keyed to each tool output's line count. Across two open-weight backbones and four multi-turn benchmarks, SWE-Pruner Pro saves up to 39% of prompt and completion tokens while preserving task quality, with bounded inference overhead. Notably, on MiMo-V2-Flash SWE-Pruner Pro additionally raises the SWE-Bench Verified resolve rate by +3.8% and the long-context Oolong accuracy by +2.2 points.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted by EACL 2027

Software Engineering.title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM
Software Engineering.summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

Software Engineering.title: GameEngineBench: Full-Session Verification of Coding Agents in a Networked Game Engine
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents face new challenges in game development, where they must produce code that is not only syntactically correct but also consistent with engine-managed lifecycle, state, and networking behavior. Existing game-development benchmarks, however, do not combine assertions over engine-based runtime states with cross-client consistency, failing to evaluate how well generated code adheres to the desired behavioral specifications. To address these limitations, we present GameEngineBench, a benchmark of 110 C++ implementation tasks derived from 9 existing Unreal Engine 5 projects. Each task requires an agent to implement missing behavior within an established gameplay architecture. We also introduce Full-Session Verification, a testing framework that injects hidden tests after the agent finishes and evaluates the resulting implementation inside Play-in-Editor (PIE) sessions, with networked client worlds in 71 tasks. The tests evaluate Unreal's game loop, actor lifecycle, subsystems, and replication stack while directly inspecting runtime state. In 53 tasks, 119 tests additionally inspect a distinct client world to determine whether the authoritative server state is correctly replicated. To our knowledge, this is the first coding benchmark to evaluate cross-client replication. Across 11 model-harness configurations, the best-scoring configuration achieves 46.4% pass@1, while 43 tasks remain unsolved by every evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate that compilation and shallow verification overestimate agents' ability to implement behavior that remains correct during full engine execution.

Software Engineering.title: Consumer-Time Validity in Stateful AI Runtimes: Verifying Recovered State and Deferred Authority
Software Engineering.summary: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.
Software Engineering.comment: 32 pages, 5 figures, 18 tables

Software Engineering.title: "What Should I Do?" Guidelines for Responsibly Integrating AI in Software Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Speculations abound about the "right" ways for developers to integrate AI into their software engineering (SE) work, but the evidence that exists is sparse and contradictory. Yet, developers are held responsible for the products they ship with (or without) AI's help, so they need to integrate AI in responsible ways. To address this gap, we conducted a two-phase, large-scale investigation with 1,118 developers at Microsoft, GitHub, and Pfizer. In Phase 1, we surveyed 860 developers at Microsoft on where they sought and resisted AI support in their daily work, and from their accounts, synthesized 35 developer-facing guidelines: 29 across five categories of SE work and 6 cross-cutting ones. A year later, as AI capabilities and developers' experiences co-evolved, we validated them in Phase 2 with 258 developers in technology (Microsoft, GitHub) and biopharmaceutical (Pfizer) domains. Developers in our study found the guidelines clearly worded (92%) and relevant to their work (91%), and most wanted to adopt them in their own work (89%). We also report how developers described operationalizing these guidelines in practice: using AI to refine their craft and delegate verifiable work, while keeping judgment and accountability for themselves. For relationship-centric work, endorsement varied with developers' domain and their SE and AI experience. Overall, we offer concrete advice from in-the-trenches developers to other in-the-trenches developers, and a shared vocabulary that engineering teams can adopt to integrate AI well in their work.

Software Engineering.title: SaltBench: A Referee-Gated Protocol for Measuring Method Effects in Machine-Checked Software Work
Software Engineering.summary: SaltBench asks how a machine referee changes how a coding agent works. Outcomes are decided outside the agent's toolchain; on the Claude lane a wall probed before any scored run isolates the agent from the network, reference solutions and harness, and 5 Gemini-lane cells served web search results are declared and leave every comparison; a dated freeze of predictions authorizes each run; a budget stop is a halt, never a failure. Five Rust systems components on a pinned Verus toolchain are each refereed by a withheld test suite. The arms: plain; salt-diet, also instructed to specify and verify its code (a registered reduced rendering of the method); and two arms handed the specification a priori, where the registered sign test at k=4 reached no verdict (3 of 4, p = 0.3125). salt-diet cost more on all five components, by a practical margin: no premium exceeded 2.8879x under either reading of the declared set and the three cheapest sat below 1.4x, a bound of this population and not a promise about larger ones: the premium is near 1 on the smallest components and rises with size. Versions 2 and 3 add the complete pilot matrix: 200 conditions over four models, 181 with a result of record, 16 inexpressible and 3 declared unreached at the cost cap, with no verdict on the arms. Version 3 adds a correctness reading, declared post hoc and registered after every verdict it reads existed and many had been read by its author: 447 cells pass the withheld suite, 40 fail, 10 are censored at a registered budget, 4 are unscorable and 42 are read by condition. salt-diet's pass-rate interval lies wholly below plain's on 8 greenfield and 5 brownfield rows and wholly above it on 2 greenfield rows. It is descriptive, over three cells of record per condition, with no test, and says nothing about whether the method makes code more or less correct. The full record is public.
Software Engineering.comment: v5: corrects the abstract's network-isolation clause, which held for the Claude lane only; adds two temp-directory limits; adds three dated sections: a second model run on the same matrix beside a same-day control, and two first-stage reads of an explanation arm. No table of record changes. 56 pages

Software Engineering.title: Micro Operational Robustness of LLMs on Code Generation
Software Engineering.summary: It is now common practice in software development for large language models (LLMs) to be used to generate program code. It is desirable to evaluate the robustness of LLMs for this usage. This paper is concerned in particular with how sensitive LLMs are to variations in descriptions of the coding tasks. However, existing techniques for evaluating this robustness are unsuitable for code generation because the input data space of natural language (NL) descriptions is discrete and sparse. To address this problem, we propose a robustness evaluation method called scenario domain analysis, which aims to find the expected minimal change in the NL descriptions of coding tasks that would cause the LLMs to produce incorrect outputs. We have formally proved the theoretical properties of the method and also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of four state-of-the-art LLMs: Gemini-pro, Codex, Llamma2 and Falcon 7B, and have found that we are able to rank these with confidence from best to worst. Moreover, we have also studied how robustness varies in different scenarios, including the variations with the topic of the coding task and with the complexity of its sample solution, and found that robustness is lower for more complex tasks and also lower for more advanced topics, such as multi-threading and data structures.

Software Engineering.title: Formally-Verifiable and Human-Interpretable RTL Generation with LLM-Guided Stepwise Refinement
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are accelerating register-transfer level (RTL) development, but ensuring the correctness of generated designs remains a major challenge. Existing LLM-driven workflows rely heavily on simulation-based verification, which provides limited correctness guarantees, and often offer little insight into the design decisions behind the generated RTL. We present a framework for LLM-guided, correct-by-construction RTL generation that combines the generative capabilities of LLMs with the mathematical rigor of stepwise refinement. The framework translates natural-language requirements into a formal hardware contract and progressively refines the contract into an implementation. At each refinement step, the LLM proposes a design decision, while the refinement engine applies the corresponding transformation only after formally verifying its correctness. The resulting program is formally verified against the contract and then translated into synthesizable RTL. The recorded derivation allows every line of generated RTL to be traced back to the design decisions and requirements that motivated it. Beyond generating verified implementations, the framework provides reliable verification feedback and reusable design experience, laying the foundation for self-improving hardware generation.

Software Engineering.title: Refined, Reliable and Reproducible: Algorithmic Analysis and Reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder
Software Engineering.summary: Cosmic voids are vast underdense regions of the Universe that encode valuable information about its large-scale structure and evolution. By extending spherical voids into overlapping sphere structures, the Popcorn Void Finder demonstrated an improved statistical characterization of cosmic void populations. However, its origin as a research prototype progressively hindered its maintainability and extensibility. Moreover, post-publication algorithmic modifications have not been systematically evaluated, leaving their statistical and computational consequences insufficiently characterized. In this work, we present a comprehensive reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder, prioritizing algorithmic transparency, maintainability, and reproducibility. We document the complete identification procedure, revisit the original algorithmic choices, and evaluate their statistical and computational consequences. Comparisons between implementations revealed a significant change in the behavior of the Void Size Function, which is now characterized by a power-law regime transitioning to a Schechter-like distribution. These changes not only provide a better characterization of void sizes, but enable a new and more robust method to the determination of the shot-noise dominated regime, without implicit dependencies on internal finder parameters present in previous works. Performance benchmarks demonstrate a 1.62x speedup in spherical void identification and a substantial improvement in overlap-removal throughput. We determined the Popcorn algorithm to be negatively affected by load imbalance, and found a speedup of 63x in a tested configuration with a newly introduced early growth termination criterion. These results establish a more maintainable and reproducible foundation for popcorn void identification, while clarifying the statistical and computational trade-offs that govern its performance.

Software Engineering.title: CivilCADBench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Understanding, Reconstructing, and Designing Civil Engineering Drawing Sets
Software Engineering.summary: Civil infrastructure is designed, built, and maintained through engineering drawing sets, yet preparing and revising them remains labour-intensive and calls for automation. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are promising candidates, but assessing them requires a benchmark grounded in real engineering practice. We introduce CivilCADBench, a benchmark for understanding, reconstructing, and designing civil engineering drawing sets, built from real infrastructure drawings and source CAD files containing over 250,000 CAD entities. Unlike parametric 3D CAD models, these drawings are dense, layered, and multi-sheet; and since prints are lossy projections with no pixel trace of layers, a file can print correctly yet remain wrongly organised. CivilCADBench comprises three task families of increasing difficulty: understanding tasks are evaluated with 2,183 expert-reviewed questions ranging from single sheets to whole sets, while reconstruction and design tasks are agentic, requiring models to rebuild printed pages as editable CAD files, either as single pages or entire drawing sets, and to produce new designs. These tasks are performed across 232 pages, 28 sets, and 19 design tasks, and evaluated by a deterministic scorer that compares model outputs with the designers' source files on geometry, layers, text, and dimensions. We evaluate seven frontier MLLMs on CivilCADBench, and find that they read and redraw printed content accurately but recover the file structure poorly: the best model scores above 90% in understanding and single-page reconstruction, yet only 60% on layer assignment and 48% on design. Grounded in real engineering practice, CivilCADBench exposes both the capabilities and the limitations of frontier models in professional civil engineering, laying a foundation for next-generation models and agentic systems for intelligent civil engineering.
Software Engineering.comment: Project page: https://agenticivil.com/civilcadbench/

Software Engineering.title: Dhaani: A Data-Flow-Driven Tool for Greenfield Construction and Brownfield Modernisation
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models can generate plausible code quickly, but an end-to-end prompt leaves developers with little control over decomposition, interfaces, or the assumptions that must survive later revisions. We present Dhaani, a free desktop application for greenfield program construction and brownfield repository modernisation. It makes an annotated data-flow diagram (ADFD) the inspectable contract between intent and implementation. In the greenfield workflow, Build, a user turns natural-language requirements into a typed graph, reviews process specifications and pre/post-conditions, ratifies generated modules, and proceeds in dependency order for Python or .NET (C#). In the brownfield workflow, Migrate uses source inference to recover an ADFD from a Fortran repository, performs target generation in bounded dependency groups, and exposes source-target alignment, generated code, errors, time, token use, and cost. The tool keeps code and artifacts on the user's machine and supports cloud or locally hosted models. Two scientific synthesis case studies produced executable systems where matched low/no-code baselines failed or were substantially less accurate. On 50 open-source Fortran repositories, the migration workflow made all 382 fixed source-oracle probes runnable and passed 327 (85.6%); two direct translation baselines each passed 83 (21.7% of planned probes). Pre-built installers and usage instructions are freely available. Tool and usage guide: https://shraddhasurana.github.io/dhaani/. Video: https://youtu.be/SShWwOMgJ9c.
Software Engineering.comment: 4 pages, 4 figures

Software Engineering.title: When the Next Step Is Not One Step: Distribution-Aware Execution Modeling for Concurrent Go Programs
Software Engineering.summary: Predicting the next scheduler event of a concurrent program is ill-posed as single-label classification: repeated runs from the same trace prefix produce different, equally valid next events. We formulate next-event prediction for concurrent Go programs as estimating an empirical next-event distribution obtained from repeated executions, and release a benchmark with 945 training examples from hand-written and generated programs and 798 held-out predictions on 54 real-world GoKer bug kernels from systems such as CockroachDB, Kubernetes, gRPC and etcd. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with low-rank adapters under a cross-entropy objective and a KL-to-empirical-distribution objective and compare them with zero-shot models and trivial baselines. The outcome is a neutral-to-negative result. The fine-tuned adapters (re-evaluated: 36.3% cross-entropy, 33.6% KL; originally reported 36.2% and 35.8%) are statistically indistinguishable from always predicting the majority event (35.5%), and an event n-gram model reaches 33-34%. Because each held-out prompt carries labels from about five runs, no deterministic predictor can exceed 58.9% top-1 accuracy, so we report macro-F1, balanced accuracy, per-class recall, program-clustered confidence intervals and binned calibration measured directly on both adapters. A sensitivity study with 100 runs per program shows that five-run targets are noisy (mean total-variation distance 0.24 from a 100-run reference), which plausibly limits what the KL objective can learn. Rare event types are essentially never predicted. A select-block goroutine-leak signature follows from scheduler semantics rather than learning. We release the data, adapters and tooling.
Software Engineering.comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for poster presentation at ICTer 2026. Substantially revised evaluation with trivial baselines, adapter re-evaluation, corrected calibration analysis, and run-count sensitivity analysis; conclusions revised accordingly

Software Engineering.title: Rule-Guided and Trajectory-Aware Repair for LLM-Based HLS Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising path for directly generating functionally correct and synthesizable HLS-C from natural-language specifications. However, existing approaches often struggle to turn multi-round tool feedback and reusable HLS knowledge into effective revisions, limiting end-to-end generation success. We propose MementoHLS, an agentic HLS generation framework built around executable and falsifiable dual-memory-guided repair. MementoHLS combines an Executable Repair Contract Library (ERCL), which converts cross-task HLS knowledge into evidence-gated repair actions, with a Reviewer-Grounded Falsification Ledger (RFL), which converts task-local repair history into trajectory evidence to suppress ineffective routes and preserve validated progress. To ensure reliable outcome attribution, a Same-Candidate Reviewer binds Parse, Compile, Testbench (TB), and Synthesis (Synth) outcomes to the corresponding candidate, while a Single-Commit Arbiter commits at most one candidate per round. Across Llama-3-8B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/32B, MementoHLS improves same-candidate TB$\wedge$Synth pass@1/pass@5 over Zero-shot by an average of 16.1/12.1 percentage points on HLS-Eval (94 tasks) and 15.1/10.4 on Bench4HLS (170 tasks). The corresponding Bench4HLS gains average 11.0/8.5 percentage points across four strong proprietary LLMs.
Software Engineering.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Revised version with an updated author list

Software Engineering.title: Verifying Autoware Controller Node by Combining Model Verification and Runtime Monitoring
Software Engineering.summary: Formal modeling and verification of autonomous driving systems remain challenging due to the vast operational space and the complexity of the control logic. We propose a hybrid verification approach that combines formal model verification and runtime monitoring for the trajectory-following control node of Autoware, an open-source autonomous driving platform. We formalize the controller as a hybrid system in differential dynamic logic (dL), and introduce an abstract model that captures the essential control dynamics. We then prove safety and liveness properties of the model using the KeYmaera X proof assistant. Complementarily, we monitor the constraints that assure the compatibility between the model and the Autoware implementation across numerical simulation runs using the Autoware toolchain, quantifying to what extent the implementation's behavior is subsumed by the verified model. The experimental results confirmed that (i) monitoring provides a sound evaluation of target following with accuracy bounds, and (ii) the Autoware implementation reaches the target with an accuracy of approximately 0.2-0.4 (m) in position and 0.8 (m/s) in velocity.
Software Engineering.comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Extended version of a paper accepted at SEFM 2026. Corrects the AWSIM monitoring results

Software Engineering.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
Software Engineering.summary: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.
Software Engineering.comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Software Engineering.title: When to Test, Repair, or Regenerate: Decision-Guided Efficient RTL Generation
