The system examined 247 students in an operating systems course (three exercises, 546 sittings, two examination languages). The grader's oral score was uncorrelated with the same submission's code quality score (Spearman rho = -0.073, 95% CI [-0.205, 0.063], n = 216) yet tracked degree grade point average (rho = 0.419, [0.294, 0.523], n = 214), while automated test scores sat at the ceiling. The mean of a student's two oral scores correlated with grade point average at 0.468 ([0.353, 0.568], n = 210), within the range of grades in three single-semester courses built on programming assignments. Model spend averaged at most $1.37 per sitting. In surveys, students began skeptical of the AI examination and rated it more favorably after sitting it twice. These results indicate that examining students on their own code is feasible at class scale, and that its score relates to academic standing where the code quality score does not.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Trajectories Through Parsons Problems: Making Student Difficulty Patterns Visible to Instructors
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Existing Parsons problem tools primarily focus on correctness, indicating whether a student solved a problem, but providing limited visibility into the underlying problem-solving process. Without that visibility, instructors cannot see which blocks caused repeated confusion or which distractors were consistently selected. We introduce Pulla, a Parsons problem tool that instruments programming assignments to capture fine-grained interaction data. We examine what these behavioral traces make visible to instructors, namely how long students take on a problem and how many moves they make, which recurring errors the distractors expose and how the class arrives at them, whether those errors follow a student from one problem to the next, and which students complete the whole assignment without a single error.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Windchime: an Audiovisual Installation with Audio-Language Model implementations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Windchime is an audiovisual installation in which spoken language retrieves music and interactive animations from an artist authored corpus. A local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model transcribes each prompt while an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape with live coded Strudel fragments that layer into audio output. Simultaneously each spoken input results in retrieval of interactive Three.js animation scenes each containing unique tactile control via monome grid and arc hardware. Windchime distributes agency in three distinct directions; across the artist who authored the possible outputs, the ALM that influences what areas of the corpus can be retrieved, and the visitor whose spoken inputs result in multimodal embodied interaction.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Creative AI Track (artwork). 4 pages (3 pages plus references), 2 figures. Video: https://youtu.be/j3XyW2ynH5Y OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=KKLTKVVHkM NeurIPS: https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/loc/sydney/160685

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Designing Algorithmic Recommendations to Achieve Human-AI Complementarity
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Algorithms frequently assist, rather than replace, human decision-makers. However, the design and analysis of algorithms often focus on predicting outcomes and do not explicitly model their effect on human decisions. This discrepancy between the design and role of algorithmic assistants becomes particularly concerning in light of empirical evidence that suggests that algorithmic assistants again and again fail to improve human decisions. In this article, we formalize the design of recommendation algorithms that assist human decision-makers without making restrictive ex-ante assumptions about how recommendations affect decisions. We formulate an algorithmic-design problem that leverages the potential-outcomes framework from causal inference to model the effect of recommendations on a human decision-maker's binary treatment choice. Within this model, we make a connection between algorithmic recommendations and instrumental variables. Leveraging this connection, we introduce a monotonicity assumption that leads to an intuitive classification of human responses to the algorithm. Under this assumption, we can express the human's response to algorithmic recommendations in terms of their compliance with the algorithm and the active decision they would take if the algorithm sends no recommendation. We showcase the utility of our framework using an online experiment that simulates a hiring task. We argue that our approach can make sense of the relative performance of different recommendation algorithms in the experiment and can help design solutions that realize human-AI complementarity. Finally, we leverage our approach to derive maximin-optimal recommendation algorithms that can be implemented with machine learning using limited training data.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Introducing ReTiNA-Cinema: Real-Time Neuro-Augmented Cinema via Generative AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is currently revolutionizing content creation across various media. Between those who fear it will replace human creativity and those who regard it solely as a tool, many in the creative industries are beginning to view generative AI as a collaborator. Yet interaction with these systems often relies on discrete, turn-based prompting that can interrupt flow and constrain expression to symbolic text. We explore physiological signals as a source of continuous adaptation without explicit commands, as a path toward embodied co-creation. This paper presents ReTiNA-Cinema, a methodological proof-of-concept that integrates electroencephalography (EEG) with generative AI to enable physiologically guided visual modulation of cinematic material. By linking physiological activity to the evolving appearance of a film, the system provides a basis for exploring embodied sense-making, in which viewers' bodily responses contribute to shaping the sensory experience through which they interpret the unfolding scenes. The system combines real-time EEG signal processing with a generative AI pipeline based on Stable Diffusion Turbo for frame-level image transformation. Single-user and two-user configurations map EEG-derived features to prompt selection and transformation strength. ReTiNA-Cinema offers a framework for exploring how the physiology of viewers might influence a film's visual presentation, extending the possibilities for participation in cinematic experiences and storytelling. This system raises questions about the effects on engagement, perceived agency, and emotional response, which remain open to future empirical study. Video illustrations: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLMu36WzSQKiVeBnrUdwUAoUhqLqGX3_bw and implementation: https://github.com/KairosHive/retina-cinema.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Rethinking Utility in Differentially Private Visualization: A Channel-Centric Perspective
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to protect sensitive data in visualization, but understanding how privacy-induced noise affects visual representations remains fragmented. Prior work has examined the impact of DP noise on specific chart types, yet these findings are typically tied to particular chart types and evaluation settings, making it difficult to generalize across contexts. In parallel, visualization research has long established that visual channels, the visual properties of marks that encode data attributes, differ in perceptual effectiveness under noise-free conditions. However, these principles have not been systematically revisited under DP, where noise is deliberately introduced into the data to protect privacy. In this paper, we present a channel-centric perspective to reframe prior empirical and theoretical results. Our synthesis drawson prior findings to motivate a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis: the utility of DP visualizations may depend on the task-relevant reads made salient by visual channel configurations and DP mechanism choice jointly. Moreover, this perspective highlights the role of channel choice throughout the privacy-preserving visualization pipeline, from disclosure framing and DP algorithm design to utility evaluation and interpretation of noisy outputs. The synthesis also identifies gaps in the existing evaluation literature and highlights research opportunities for channel-aware DP visualization.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A human-in-the-loop Bayesian optimization framework for constraint-aware bioprocess development
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We present Pareto Front Guided Sampling (PFGS), a human-in-the-loop (HiL) Bayesian Optimization (BO) framework that reformulates surrogate-model predictions as a multi-objective optimization problem, allowing domain knowledge to beadded intuitively to any BO problem. PFGS addresses constrained optimization by treating the posterior probability of constraint satisfaction as an explicit Pareto objective, and robust optimization via a Monte Carlo estimate of expected lower-confidence performance under input perturbations, capturing likely degradation. The multi-dimensional Pareto front makes trade-offs between predicted performance, model uncertainty, constraint satisfaction, and robustness visible through pairwise two-dimensional projections on an interactive dashboard, allowing selection criteria to be refined as the model and objectives evolve. The framework is showcased on a eight-dimensional in-silico fed-batch Chinese Hamster Ovary cell culture case study. We showed improved performance over BO when the expert has perfect domain knowledge; however, PFGS is not designed to outperform BO, but rather to present a HiL acquisition function framework.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: RouterWeave: A Unified Observation Layer for Cross-Platform Activity Analysis via Home Routers
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Smart homes bring together devices from different operating systems and vendor ecosystems, but each platform reports activity only for the devices and features it supports, leaving gaps in household-wide activity monitoring. Interoperability standards such as Matter and software integrations connect and control supported devices, yet vendor restrictions and licensing barriers limit access to their data, while hardware constraints hinder integration. Our key insight is that encrypted network traffic provides complementary evidence of activity across platform boundaries. Accordingly, we present RouterWeave, a router-side observation framework that combines cross-platform traffic collection, task-adaptive processing, and unified activity records. These records preserve activity meaning, temporal extent, and source-device attribution while distinguishing discrete operations from sustained activity intervals. We evaluate RouterWeave across four datasets, native execution on a commodity home router, and two novel case studies: cross-platform Screen Time monitoring and appliance energy estimation. RouterWeave achieves 94.41% macro-F1 on application activities and 97.46% on IoT operations, outperforming baselines by up to 20.99 percentage points, while using under 7 MB of router memory per task and supporting 54 concurrent devices within a 5-second update window. In end-to-end case studies, RouterWeave reconstructs 600 Screen Time timelines across Android, iOS, and Windows with 92.15% accuracy (24.84-second mean active-time error over 19-minute averages) and recovers 49 of 55 appliance operations over four days, tracking ON/OFF states with 92.84% agreement and estimating electricity use within a 4.28% error. Together, these results establish the commodity home router as practical infrastructure for whole-home activity sensing. The code is open sourced at https://github.com/naisslab/routerweave.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Presenting Your Figures: Data-informed Animated Transitions Across Scientific Figure Panels
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Multi-panel figures are commonly used in research papers to show scientific data, and researchers often reuse them when presenting their work. Presenting these figures often involves explaining how data across chart panels are related. Animated transitions can progressively reveal these relationships, but two static panels specify only the endpoints, leaving what intermediate keyframes should show and how the transition should progress unclear. To support transition design across diverse scientific figures, we developed Figure Space and Transition Space through iterative analysis of 48 published multi-panel figures across eight scientific subject areas. Figure Space represents panel composition, data transformations, and visual encodings while retaining the links needed to trace panel results back to records. Transition Space uses this representation and source data to construct and sequence keyframes that make corresponding data visible and align them while preserving the meaning of each panel's position encodings. Building on these spaces, we developed FigFlux, a human-in-the-loop authoring system that guides AI agents in generating animated transitions from a multi-panel figure and its associated materials. Researchers can revise keyframes in natural language before animation generation. We evaluate FigFlux through cross-domain case studies, a study with 16 scientific authors, and expert assessment. Authors reported lower overall workload than with their familiar tools, while experts gave FigFlux transitions higher ratings than transitions created with participants' familiar tools or generated by AI alone. The example gallery have been published online: https://figflux.github.io.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Profiling Handwriting-Process Deviations in Developmental Dysgraphia: An Open, Normatively-Referenced Instrument
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Online handwriting captured on digitizing tablets yields hundreds of kinematic, temporal, spatial, and dynamic features. These features are rarely organized into interpretable, reusable constructs, and, although standardized tests norm the handwritten product, no openly available instrument places a child's handwriting process relative to a verified-typical reference. We introduce and validate an open measurement instrument for profiling handwriting-process deviations in children with developmental dysgraphia from sentence-level online handwriting. The instrument comprises (i)~a literature-only vocabulary, fixed before any cohort analysis, organizing 136 online-handwriting features into 12 handwriting-process domains, and (ii)~an age- and sex-adjusted normative reference framework, fit on verified-typical children only, that turns those features into a 12-axis deviation profile with per-child bootstrap uncertainty. We establish its measurement properties on the DiaGraMo cohort (N=257 Czech children aged 8--12; 110 verified-typical, 147 with dysgraphia): the vocabulary is structurally coherent, and the reference is calibrated, parsimonious, and leakage-free. On the same cohort, five of twelve domains separate the groups at BH~$q<.05$ (Cliff's~$δ$ +0.19 to +0.51), on spatial, temporal, and pen-orientation processes, and 96.5\% of participant~$\times$~domain scores have a bootstrap CI narrower than one z-unit. No classifier is trained: the instrument reports uncertainty-aware deviation scores rather than a diagnostic label, and its outlier rate is not a diagnostic rate. The vocabulary, the analysis code, and an open reference implementation that scores new participants are all openly released, giving handwriting and dysgraphia researchers a reusable, validated instrument for situating individual children against a normative reference.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Ground Truth Bias in AI-Assisted Medical Annotation: A Crossover Study Using an Independent Radiologist Reference Standard
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Behavioural evaluations of artificial-intelligence-assisted annotation score every human decision against a reference standard, so their conclusions inherit that standard's validity. We tested how far conclusions about assistance, reliance and individual differences depend on it. Fifty-one non-expert high-school students annotated 50 knee radiographs for osteoarthritis, with and without a deliberately imperfect classifier, in a crossover design; personality and non-verbal reasoning were also measured. Decisions were scored against the public repository labels and against an independent reference standard from a radiologist panel, which graded 23 of the 50 images as indeterminate. Against the repository labels, assistance raised accuracy from 60.4% to 65.3% (odds ratio 1.23, p=0.002). Against the independent standard, the gain on the 27 determinate images was smaller and not significant in the primary model (78.4% to 80.8%; odds ratio 1.16, p=0.178). The apparent benefit had been concentrated on the indeterminate images and was not significant when those images were assigned to either class. The direction of residual over-reliance depended on how indeterminate cases were handled, and the personality trait most strongly associated with accuracy changed identity and sign between standards. Reliance measures are only as valid as the reference standard that defines when the assistant is right.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Embodied Human-Data Interaction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We propose the concept of human-data interaction (HDI) as the human manipulation, analysis, and sensemaking of large, unstructured, and complex datasets. We then proceed to suggest an embodied approach to HDI to build physical reasoning environments for these difficult and polymorphic tasks. We illustrate our approach with two examples: tangible lenses for visual exploration, and an educational computer game with tangible bricks.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Published May 2011 at the Embodied Interaction: Theory and Practice in HCI at ACM CHI 2011

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Reliance to Overreliance: Taxonomizing and Detecting Relational Risks in AI Companionship
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic Character.AI and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MetaScanner: An Empirical Study and Proactive Defense against Deceptive UI Attacks in Social VR
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Social virtual reality (VR) platforms have surged in popularity but continue to face significant security challenges, including privacy invasion and user manipulation. Yet, the security risks posed by deceptive content remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce four novel deceptive UI attacks that covertly manipulate social VR users into performing unintended actions without their awareness. We show how adversarial content creators can embed seemingly benign scripts and interactive elements within carefully designed virtual worlds, deceiving users into unknowingly carrying out harmful behaviors. We implemented these attacks on VRChat, a leading social VR platform, and an IRB-approved user study involving 30 participants confirmed their effectiveness. To mitigate these threats, we propose MetaScanner, a proactive analysis system that efficiently scans virtual world assets, including scripts and interactive objects, to identify suspicious or deceptive elements before users are exposed to them. We demonstrate that MetaScanner can successfully detect all threats in test worlds where the four attack scenarios were implemented. Additionally, MetaScanner shows its lightweight nature, with an average scanning time of 5 seconds across 38 real-world assets.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 23 pages, 21 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to Computers & Security. This is the authors' accepted manuscript

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing.
  Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust.
  Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale.
  Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts.
  Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Sycamore: Grounded Synthetic Evaluation for Visualization Systems
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Evaluating visualization systems in specialized domains, such as genomics, is challenging due to the scarcity of domain experts and difficulty recruiting relevant user types. LLM-based synthetic personas provide an appealing workaround, but they face skepticism as their claims often lack verifiable grounding. We present Sycamore, an exploratory approach to evaluating visualization systems with grounded synthetic personas whose responses are restricted to interview evidence. Sycamore enforces provenance with participant citations for each claim and an abstention mechanism when retrieval yields no relevant evidence. A protocol runner guides the synthetic personas through an evaluation of the live visualization system, producing multi-turn transcripts for qualitative coding. We instantiate the approach on Geranium, a multimodal genomics visualization search engine, with seven evaluators grounded in prior interviews on genomics visualization authoring. We report themes in the resulting transcripts, highlight an emergent requirement absent from the source data, and provide a preliminary comparison to a prior human user study. Recognizing that our findings derive from an exploratory perspective and that synthetic proxies cannot replace human evaluation, we discuss their implications for integrating synthetic evaluators alongside expert user studies. The protocol, codebook, extended results, transcripts, and demo video are in the Supplementary Materials and at https://osf.io/kdfr3/; the source code and project page are at https://huyen-nguyen.github.io/sycamore/.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Presented at the VISxGenAI Workshop at IEEE VIS 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, 14 tables, including supplementary material

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "I Talked to an AI Chatbot, So What's Next?" How U.S. Young Adults Imagine Responsible AI for Emotion Coping
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Emotion coping is inherently relational, unfolding through interactions with friends, family, professionals, and communities. Yet AI chatbots are largely designed around a user--AI dyad. Learning from the ethics of care, we examine how AI chatbots shape the relational conditions of emotion coping. We conducted a scenario-based study with 17 U.S. young adults across four emotion coping scenarios. Participants identified eight roles through which AI could support relational conditions, alongside three challenges: flattening distinct relational conditions, discouraging reciprocity, and shifting relational labor onto users. This study contributed a relational perspective of responsible AI in emotion coping. We argue that responsible AI should respond to individuals' situated relational conditions rather than provide general-purpose support. We further identify two design principles: fostering reciprocity by supplying materials to engage with others, and strengthening emotional self-efficacy. Together, we position responsible AI as AI in the loop of human relationships.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: GenAI-DBT: Evaluating a DBT-Informed Generative AI Platform for Mindfulness Skills Training: A Pilot Randomized Study
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and engagement of three digital formats for dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) mindfulness skills training. In a 30-day randomized pilot study, 45 university students were assigned to GenAI-DBT, a general-purpose large language model chatbot (Chatbot), or a static web resource (Web). Forty-two completed the study, and nine completed follow-up interviews. Usability scores were within acceptable ranges across conditions, with no significant between-group differences. GenAI-DBT showed the highest observed participant-week adherence (71.4%, vs. 53.3% for Web and 42.3% for Chatbot), a descriptive difference. Mindful Attention Awareness Scale and Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale scores showed no significant time-by-group interactions, and session-level self-reported mood changes did not differ significantly across conditions. GenAI-DBT showed a larger positive change in linguistic valence than Chatbot (4.28 vs. 1.59, P = .02, Cohen's d = 0.99). Interviewees valued contextualized, scenario-based practice and identified response latency, repetition, and limited personalization as areas for improvement. The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of DBT-informed conversational AI for skills practice and motivate further evaluation in larger, more clinically relevant samples. Clinical efficacy remains to be established.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Jingchen Ye, Yujia Chen, and Leyang Han contributed equally. Yucheng Jin is the corresponding author

Human-Computer Interaction.title: VideoTrail: Interactive Video Foraging Through Hierarchical Visualization
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: People often watch videos to find information, but locating relevant moments can be difficult and time-consuming. Existing strategies like scrubbing rely primarily on visual scanning and linear search, providing limited support for goal-directed navigation. We present VideoTrail, an AI-powered browser extension that supports information seeking in videos through a hierarchical visualization. Inspired by information foraging theory, VideoTrail surfaces semantic and structural cues as information scent, creating an explorable roadmap of segments. The system is multimodal and adaptive, prioritizing visual or textual scent based on the video's content. In a user study (N=16), VideoTrail helped participants efficiently locate key moments and enabled new navigation strategies compared to traditional timelines, highlighting how exposing an adaptive video structure can enhance goal-directed viewing.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Map2Video: Guiding Real-World-Grounded AI Video Generation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI video generation lowers barriers to video creation, but existing tools provide limited support for grounding content in real-world locations, restricting their use in applications such as film previsualization and scenario generation. In practice, users rely on verbose textual descriptions or reference images using on-site photos or street view imagery (SVI), which are cumbersome and unreliable across shots. Our formative study with five filmmakers revealed challenges in shot composition, character motion, and camera control when using SVI with an image-to-video tool. We present Map2Video, a system for guiding SVI-grounded AI video generation through map-based character trajectory annotation and direct manipulation of cameras and character masks defined in geodetic coordinates and projected onto panoramic screen coordinates. In an evaluation with twelve filmmakers, Map2Video provided stronger controllability for both scene replication and open-ended creative exploration, reduced cognitive effort, and improved spatial consistency across multiple shots compared to an image-to-video baseline.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 16 pages, 7 tables, 5 figures, 1 appendix. Companion paper: arXiv:2607.22397. Code: pip install nimbus-bci (v0.9.0)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Modeling Learner-Technology Interaction Through Multilevel Gaze Transition Dynamics to Inform Usability in Online Learning
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Gaze data provide fine-grained evidence of how learners engage with instructional content and interface elements, complementing conventional usability evaluation methods. However, eye-tracking analyses often examine within-slide visual attention and across-slide navigation separately, limiting understanding of learner interaction throughout extended learning experiences. This exploratory multi-method study integrated area-of-interest transitions, gaze entropy, slide-level navigation, and network-based representations to analyze seven eye-tracking recordings of high school students interacting with an AI-supported online biology lesson, complemented by three post-intervention focus groups. Results showed individual differences in within-slide gaze allocation and switching patterns. Learners followed shared navigation pathways but differed in revisiting and immediate return behaviors. The focus group findings highlighted positive perceptions of interactive materials and AI-generated feedback, alongside usability concerns related to navigation, interface clarity, and assessment guidance. Together, these outcomes show how integrating multilevel gaze analytics with learner perspectives can provide complementary evidence for identifying interaction trends relevant to usability evaluation. Future research should test this approach with larger, more diverse samples and examine relationships among gaze patterns, usability, and learning outcomes.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI-Induced Social Erosion: Using LLMs for Work Tasks Reduces Help-Seeking Intentions Towards Colleagues
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI is becoming embedded in knowledge work as an intelligent collaborator to assist in completing tasks. However, this readily available assistance risks displacing key interactions through which colleague relationships are built and sustained at work. This paper leverages the concept of help-seeking behaviour to investigate whether and how AI usage shapes colleague relationships. We conducted an online experimental vignette study where 248 knowledge workers evaluated scenarios that systematically varied whether and how AI was used across different work tasks. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that AI-enabled work reduced help-seeking intentions compared to non-AI work across tasks, and especially for brainstorming. Visible AI usage was associated with greater help-seeking intentions towards colleagues, and individual contributors' colleague relationships were more vulnerable than managers. Our findings identify opportunities for workplace AI tools, practices, and policies to preserve colleague relationships in increasingly AI-integrated workplaces.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Design and Evaluation of a Body-Machine Interface as an Alternative Control Paradigm for Pedal-based Sewing Machines
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Body-machine interfaces (BoMIs) exploit body movements to control assistive devices; they have been evaluated primarily in tasks such as cursor control or robotic manipulation where the entire movement repertoire is devoted toward device control. However, tasks with multiple concurrent processes require the user to share the movement repertoire used for device control with other body movements for task execution. This issue is examined here in the context of sewing, where the sewing machine is typically controlled by a pedal in coordination with hand movements for guiding the fabric. We evaluated the learning of a trunk-controlled BoMI for sewing machine control, and compared it with conventional pedal control. Twenty-four novice participants (12 BoMI, 12 Pedal) completed 10 trials of a standardized sewing assessment followed by 3 trials of a transfer task. The BoMI mapped trunk movements to the sewing machine's full functional repertoire, which included continuous speed control of the needle, and discrete actions such as presser-foot and needle lifts. The two groups learned at comparable rates, showing similar completion times and error counts; for both groups, completion time reduced by approximately 30\%. Additional analyses showed that the BoMI group had fewer presser-foot lift errors during training and fewer errors on the first transfer trial. Both groups also exhibited similar subjective workload. These findings collectively demonstrate that a BoMI interface can support sewing-machine control during concurrent manual activity, highlighting the potential for using BoMIs for increasing accessibility in industrial workplace contexts.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Towards Restorative Urban Spaces: An Exploratory Field Study of Nature Videos on Public Multi-Display Signage
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In recent years, multi-display signage (MDS) has become increasingly common in urban stations, plazas, and other public spaces, where it is primarily used to present advertisements and information. Beyond these conventional applications, MDS offers opportunities to shape people's experiences of public environments through spatially distributed and dynamic visual content. Motivated by the potential of mediated nature to support restorative experiences in urban environments, we conducted a nine-day exploratory field study in a free-admission area of a science museum, presenting artificial intelligence (AI)-generated nature videos across four displays and collecting 1,263 questionnaire responses. We combined three complementary analyses. First, structural equation modeling identified strong associations among perceived consistency across displays, presence, and self-reported restorative responses, consistent with our theoretically motivated model. Second, exploratory comparisons across video-presentation configurations revealed modest differences in consistency and restoration ratings, although these AI-generated videos did not significantly outperform the advertisement reference. Third, qualitative analysis of open-ended responses identified fascination, immersion, and restorative feelings, alongside concerns about naturalness, visual quality, and motion-related discomfort. Together, these findings provide empirical insights into MDS-mediated nature experiences, with implications for nature-video design and questionnaire refinement. They also inform a tentative conceptual extension of the model incorporating additional perceptual and evaluative factors.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Crisis Governance at the Joints. Mapping the Ethical and Societal Territory of Crisis Management Technologies: The Case of Human-Swarm Teaming
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI-Assisted Hypothesis Generation for Hospital Quality Improvement
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Hospital quality improvement (QI) programs generally proceed in two stages: (1) hypothesis generation, which identifies candidate factors that may improve care quality and efficiency, and (2) confirmatory analyses, which implement and evaluate QI initiatives targeting these factors. Although most research focuses on the confirmatory stage, hypothesis generation is equally important because it shapes where teams focus their effort. Currently, hypothesis generation depends on expert-driven, qualitative methods (e.g., Lean Healthcare tools) that can be anecdotal, hard to reproduce, time-consuming, and resource-intensive. Large language models (LLMs) could accelerate this process by analyzing clinical notes at scale, but existing AI tools can only scale up well-defined tasks, whereas hypothesis generation is a "fuzzy," exploratory, and iterative process. We propose treating not only LLM instructions but also the problem specification and validation process as tunable natural-language (hyper)parameters. Through a procedure we term "Human-AI Spec-Solution Co-Optimization," we iteratively elicit clinical experts' definitions and judgments while aligning the AI pipeline with their intended criteria. We retrospectively applied this framework at an urban safety-net hospital to length of stay and 30-day unplanned readmissions. The final pipelines screen patient charts for potential factors and filter for clinically relevant ones by self-rating, and these self-ratings achieved over 70% concordance with human experts (within one Likert point) on held-out encounters. When scaled up hospital-wide, the pipelines identified a superset of the candidate factors found in prior, primarily manual analyses. By providing auditable reasoning traces and quantifying factor prevalence, the pipelines support a more quantitative and reproducible way to prioritize factors for prospective QI interventions.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Open Response Explorer: a Structured Collaborative Writing System for Peer-Informed Open-Response Assignments
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Peer-informed open-response assignments (where students view, connect, and learn from peer contributions) hold the potential to foster collaborative knowledge building, yet the unstructured nature of free-form prose prevents students from effectively comparing and making sense of peers' work. We present Open Response Explorer, an interface that recenters open responses on structured idea units through purpose-based writing and peer response exploration, augmented by common-role text segment highlighting for easy comparison. A within-subjects lab study (N=12) validated the usefulness and usability of the system, demonstrating how it shaped the open-response drafting and peer exploration practices. We discuss implications for purpose-centered authoring and exploration that transform free-form prose into structured, comparable, and collectively navigable knowledge artifacts.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Quasi-experimental Study of Conversational AI-supported Engagement in Large CS Courses
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Lucrative career prospects and creative opportunities often attract students to enroll in computer science courses, resulting in large class sizes. A common challenge in large classrooms is the lack of engagement between students and both the instructor and the learning material. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) present an opportunity to leverage Conversational Artificial Intelligence (CAI) to address this challenge. To examine the potential of CAI to support engagement with learning material, we designed an in class activity in a large Software Engineering course in which students interacted with a CAI tool. Using a quasi-experimental, within-subject study design in a real classroom at a large public United States University. We compared student engagement during an activity that involved the use of CAI for discussion with an activity that did not (peer discussion). For our analysis, we collected data on students interactions with the CAI tool and their self-reported responses on multiple engagement scales. Results show higher student engagement with the learning material in the activity involving CAI discussion as opposed to without (peer discussion). Higher self-reported learning was also observed in the activity with CAI as compared to without. Students also reported significantly more usefulness for learning in the CAI condition. Overall, our results indicate that CAI (ChatGPT) has the potential to support engagement with learning content during in-class activities in large class sizes.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Does AI Assistance Preserve or Collapse Disagreement? A Study of Pre-Annotations in Ambiguous Video Labeling
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
AI-generated Pre-Annotations can accelerate video labeling, but they may also anchor annotators to model priors and suppress disagreement that is valuable for pluralistic dataset construction. We study this tradeoff in ambiguous temporal video annotation, where annotators choose event boundaries and assign context-dependent labels such as "normal" or "abnormal." We introduce a controlled audit protocol that separates annotation cost, consensus alignment, inter-annotator consistency, temporal-boundary variation, semantic-label variation, latent-space standardization, and edit behavior.
  In a counterbalanced pilot study with 18 annotators and 180 annotation sessions, a fixed CLIP-based Pre-Annotation engine reduced mean annotation time by 23.11%; 72% of annotators were faster with assistance, with a median per-annotator gain of 35%. Assistance increased inter-annotator consistency and CLIP-space standardization, while semantic-label entropy changed only slightly in aggregate. A six-annotator human consensus diagnostic showed comparable alignment across conditions (AMI $\approx 0.64$ in both conditions), but this diagnostic is self-including and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as independent evidence that model influence is absent. Overall, the results suggest that Pre-Annotations acted mainly as editable temporal scaffolds in this pilot setting, while leaving open the possibility of subtler semantic anchoring effects. We contribute an audit framework and anonymized interaction traces for studying when AI-assisted annotation preserves, reshapes, or collapses human disagreement.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Human-Centric Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Digital Twin Framework for Cyber-Physical Systems
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Digital twins of cyber-physical systems must operate with scarce data, on assets that change after deployment, and for humans whose needs differ, yet existing implementations fix fidelity at design time and do not match the representation to the human or the task. This paper proposes a human-centric adaptive multi-fidelity digital twin framework that models the evolving human, the physical twin, and the digital twin core, and adds a human inference and adaptation function that estimates the human state, predicts the response, and adapts the representation. The framework defines low-, medium-, and high-fidelity tiers distinguished by adaptivity and by coupling, quantified as the ratio of the digital twin latency to the duration of the process step it follows. Three proof-of-concept instantiations are evaluated: a virtual reality tutor, a computer numerical control milling model, and an industrial training station. The low tier estimated learner sentiment with an accuracy of 0.86. The forecasters of the milling model and the training station, both medium-tier, showed a normalized error decline of 0.39 to 0.89 and a human adaptation gain of 1.16 to 1.51, but their latency exceeded the physical process step by 25 to 87 times. Only the station's vision model met the physical step. The tiers are separated by which functions adapt and where the latency constraint lies, not by a monotone increase in gain or coupling.
